docs.title: Data model & querying
docs.text: The server keeps your data in the archive: the folder given by -archive-dir (HKR_ARCHIVE_DIR), e.g. /var/lib/healthkit-relay, or ./data next to the Docker Compose file. This page says what the archive holds, how it is laid out, and how to read it with DuckDB. For a program that reads over the network, such as a dashboard, see the query API. Words such as paired device and admin token are defined in the glossary.

docs.title: What is synced
docs.text:
The app reads every type of data HealthKit offers on the phone. Its type list is generated from the iOS SDK it is built with: an app built with a newer Xcode reads the new types too. With the iOS 27 SDK that is over 200 types:

  • Quantities (heart rate, HRV, resting heart rate, walking heart rate, VO2 max, steps, distance, active and basal energy, blood oxygen, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, body mass, nutrition, audio exposure, mobility...), each with one unit for its whole history and the individual values of series samples;
  • Categories (sleep stages, symptoms, cycle tracking, mindful minutes, high/low heart rate and irregular rhythm events...), with value names;
  • Workouts with activities, events, per-type statistics and routes (every GPS point);
  • Heartbeat series, ECGs (every voltage sample, classification), audiograms;
  • Correlations (blood pressure, food) with their members;
  • State of Mind, GAD-7 / PHQ-9, medications and dose events, vision prescriptions; Health Records (FHIR) and CDA documents in builds of your own with Health Records turned on (the App Store app leaves clinical records out);
  • daily activity summaries (rings and goals) and characteristics (date of birth, biological sex, blood type...).

Every sample keeps its UUID, start and end, source (app and version), device and metadata, exactly as sent. Most kinds also carry Apple's own serialized object (NSKeyedArchiver), which keeps the properties that have no field of their own. A sample you delete in Apple Health is deleted in the archive too.

The format the app sends is documented in the server README.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Everything lives in the archive directory:

<archive-dir>/
  staging.db                 SQLite: batches not flushed yet, the de-duplication index, tombstones
  admin.json                 the admin token's SHA-256
  devices.json               paired devices and read tokens (SHA-256 of each token)
  codes.json                 setup codes not used yet (SHA-256 of each code)
  parquet/
    samples/type=HKQuantityTypeIdentifierHeartRate/month=2026-10/c1234.parquet
    samples/type=.../month=.../f5678.parquet     an hourly flush, not compacted yet
    records/type=activity_summary/month=2026-10/...
    route_points/type=HKWorkoutRouteTypeIdentifier/month=.../...
    heartbeats/type=HKDataTypeIdentifierHeartbeatSeries/month=.../...
    ecg_voltages/type=HKDataTypeIdentifierElectrocardiogram/month=.../...
    quantity_series/type=HKQuantityTypeIdentifierStepCount/month=.../...
    */type=_/month=_/schema.parquet              zero rows: queries work before any data arrives
    deleted/deleted.parquet                      tombstones
  • Write path. The server checks a whole batch, then commits it to staging.db (written to disk with fsync) before it answers the app with 200. De-duplication uses an index on disk of every record ever stored, so memory use stays the same as history grows, and a batch sent twice is stored once.
  • Flush, hourly (-flush-interval). Staged rows are written into a new Parquet file per dataset, type and month, f<seq>.parquet, then removed from staging.
  • Compaction, nightly (-compact-at, 03:30 local time by default). Each partition with more than one file is merged into one, c<seq>.parquet, and samples deleted in Apple Health are dropped from the files on the way. Months that received nothing keep their files as they are.
  • Partitions. month is the month of the sample's start, in UTC (YYYY-MM). type is the HealthKit type identifier, or the record kind in records.

Flush, compaction and erase are journaled and atomic (temp file, fsync, rename): after a crash, every record is there once. DuckDB can read the files while the server runs.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
samples and records: uuid, type, kind, key (records), start, end (timestamps, UTC), value (double), unit, source_name, source_bundle, source_version, device, uploader (the paired device's ID; empty for uploads with the admin token), wire (wire format, 1 or 2), received_at, and json, the record exactly as the app sent it, with the fields that have no column (metadata, category value names, Apple's serialized object). In records, type is the record kind (activity_summary, characteristics, medication, series...) and uuid the sample a chunk belongs to.

The series datasets have one row per point, joined to samples.uuid by sample_uuid, and ordered by chunk then i:

Dataset Columns route_points sample_uuid, chunk, i, time, lat, lon, alt, h_acc, v_acc, speed, speed_acc, course, course_acc, ellipsoidal_alt, floor heartbeats sample_uuid, chunk, i, time, t (seconds since the sample's start), gap ecg_voltages sample_uuid, chunk, i, time, t, microvolts (lead I) quantity_series sample_uuid, chunk, i, start, end, value, unit deleted uuid, wire, type, reason, uploader, received_at, json

Every point dataset also has uploader and received_at; with hive_partitioning, DuckDB adds type and month from the folder names.

Parquet is a compressed file format for tables. DuckDB, pandas, Polars, Spark, ClickHouse and most data tools read it, with or without Health Relay.

docs.title: Erasing
docs.text: Erase Server Data and Start Over, in the app's Advanced screen (the gear), calls DELETE /v1/data?confirm=erase. The server permanently deletes everything that iPhone uploaded: it rewrites the Parquet files without its rows (or removes them), deletes its staged rows, tombstones and de-duplication entries, and truncates SQLite's log. The app then uploads its history again. Erase Server Data and Disconnect sends DELETE /v1/data?confirm=erase&disconnect=1: the same erase, and the server revokes the iPhone's token in the same step, so nothing it sent before can arrive afterwards. Two copies stay as they are: numbers already forwarded to a metrics database (they age out with its retention), and copies outside the archive directory, such as backups and snapshots. With the admin token, ?confirm=erase is required, and ?device=<id> erases one paired device's data.

docs.title: Querying with DuckDB
docs.text:
DuckDB is a database program that reads the Parquet files where they are. You run it on the computer that holds the archive.

  1. Install DuckDB: brew install duckdb on macOS, or download the command-line program from duckdb.org. Check it with duckdb --version: it prints a version such as v1.5.0.

  2. Download the views, the table definitions for the archive:

    curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leblancfg/healthkit-relay/main/server/sql/views.sql

    This saves views.sql in the current folder.

  3. Go to the archive directory and start DuckDB with the views. On Linux and NixOS the archive belongs to the server's user, so open a root shell first (replace /home/you with the folder you downloaded views.sql to):

    sudo -s
cd /var/lib/healthkit-relay
duckdb -init /home/you/views.sql

    With Docker Compose and on macOS, the archive is yours: cd to it (e.g. cd data next to docker-compose.yml) and run duckdb -init ~/views.sql. DuckDB shows its prompt, D.

  4. Type a query and press Enter:

    SELECT type, count(*) AS n FROM samples GROUP BY type ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 3;

    DuckDB prints a table:

    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────┐
│                    type                    │    n    │
│                  varchar                   │  int64  │
├────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────┤
│ HKQuantityTypeIdentifierHeartRate          │ 1204311 │
│ HKQuantityTypeIdentifierStepCount          │  402118 │
│ HKQuantityTypeIdentifierActiveEnergyBurned │  398765 │
└────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────┘

  5. Type .quit to leave DuckDB (then exit to leave the root shell).

The views are samples, records, records_latest (the latest version of a record that changes, such as today's activity summary), route_points, heartbeats, ecg_voltages, quantity_series and deleted. They hide what was deleted in Apple Health and is still in the files until the nightly compaction. A query that filters on type and month reads only the matching files.

DESCRIBE samples;

-- What is there, and how much.
SELECT type, count(*) AS n, min(start) AS first, max(start) AS last
FROM samples GROUP BY type ORDER BY n DESC;

-- Daily resting heart rate.
SELECT date_trunc('day', timezone('America/New_York', start)) AS day, avg(value) AS resting_hr
FROM samples WHERE type = 'HKQuantityTypeIdentifierRestingHeartRate'
GROUP BY day ORDER BY day;

-- Heart rate variability (SDNN), weekly median, last year.
SELECT date_trunc('week', start) AS week, median(value) AS hrv_ms
FROM samples WHERE type = 'HKQuantityTypeIdentifierHeartRateVariabilitySDNN'
  AND start > now() - INTERVAL 1 YEAR
GROUP BY week ORDER BY week;

-- Hours asleep per night, by stage (the stage name is in the sample as sent).
SELECT date_trunc('day', timezone('America/New_York', "end")) AS night,
       json_extract_string(json, '$.value_label') AS stage,
       round(sum(epoch("end") - epoch(start)) / 3600, 2) AS hours
FROM samples WHERE type = 'HKCategoryTypeIdentifierSleepAnalysis'
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY night, stage;

-- Steps per day and source (iPhone and Watch both count steps).
SELECT date_trunc('day', start) AS day, source_name, sum(value) AS steps
FROM samples WHERE type = 'HKQuantityTypeIdentifierStepCount'
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY day;

-- A workout route.
SELECT time, lat, lon, alt, speed FROM route_points
WHERE sample_uuid = '<route uuid>' ORDER BY chunk, i;

-- Activity rings, latest version of each day.
SELECT json_extract_string(json, '$.date') AS day,
       json_extract(json, '$.values.active_energy_burned.value')::double AS kcal
FROM records_latest WHERE type = 'activity_summary' ORDER BY day;

Records received in the last hour may still be in staging.db only. To write them to Parquet at once, stop the server and run healthkit-relay flush with its -archive-dir.

Export anything to CSV or another Parquet file:

COPY (SELECT * FROM samples WHERE type = 'HKWorkoutTypeIdentifier')
TO 'workouts.csv' (HEADER);

From Python, started in the archive directory (the views use paths relative to it):

import duckdb
con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute(open("/path/to/views.sql").read())
df = con.sql("""
    SELECT start, value FROM samples
    WHERE type = 'HKQuantityTypeIdentifierHeartRate'
""").df()

Sum versus average

Steps, distance and energy add up: sum them. An iPhone and an Apple Watch carried together both count the same steps, so keep one source per moment, for instance one source_name. The query API's aggregates do this the way Apple Health does. Heart rate, HRV and similar are single measurements: average them.

docs.title: Metrics forwarding
docs.text:
With -forward-url set, the server also posts each new numeric sample to a metrics database as InfluxDB line protocol, after it is stored:

Sample Line quantity healthkit,source=…,unit=count/min heart_rate=62 <start> category healthkit,source=…,value=asleepDeep sleep_analysis_seconds=1800 <start> (duration) workout healthkit,activity=running,source=… workout_duration_seconds=…, workout_energy_kcal, workout_distance_meters activity summary healthkit,unit=kcal activity_summary_active_energy_burned=512 <day start>

Field names are the HealthKit identifier in snake case (HKQuantityTypeIdentifierHeartRateVariabilitySDNN → heart_rate_variability_sdnn). Routes, ECGs, documents and the other data without a number stay in the archive only. When forwarding fails, the server logs it and counts it in healthkit_relay_forward_errors_total; the upload still succeeds. See Grafana.

docs.title: How do I export Apple Health data to my own server?
docs.text:
Run the Health Relay server on a computer you own, then pair the Health Relay iPhone app with it once:

  1. Start the server, e.g. with Docker:

    mkdir -p data
docker run -d --name healthkit-relay --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 8080:8080 --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -e HKR_PUBLIC_URL=http://192.168.1.10:8080 \
  -v "$PWD/data:/data" \
  ghcr.io/leblancfg/healthkit-relay:latest

    docker logs healthkit-relay shows the admin token.

  2. Open the server's setup page in a browser, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup, sign in with the admin token, and scan the QR code with the iPhone camera.

  3. Allow Health access in the app.

The app uploads your whole Apple Health history first, then new data several times a day. The quick start walks through each step with what you should see.

docs.title: Is there a self-hosted Apple Health sync?
docs.text: Health Relay is one: the iPhone app sends HealthKit data only to the server address you pair it with, a server you run at home, on a NAS or on a rented machine. The server is one Go program, published as a Docker image and as binaries for Linux, macOS and FreeBSD, with setup guides for Docker, systemd, NixOS, macOS, Synology, Unraid, TrueNAS and Raspberry Pi.

docs.title: How do I get HealthKit data into Grafana?
docs.text:
Have the server forward numbers to a time-series database, and point Grafana at that database. With the Docker Compose file, VictoriaMetrics and Grafana come preconfigured:

echo HKR_FORWARD_URL=http://victoriametrics:8428/influx/write >> .env
docker compose --profile metrics up -d

In Grafana, healthkit_heart_rate charts your heart rate. The Grafana page covers dashboards, queries and setups without Compose.

docs.title: Can I send Apple Health data to InfluxDB or VictoriaMetrics?
docs.text:
Yes. The server forwards every numeric sample (heart rate, HRV, steps, sleep durations, VO2 max...) in InfluxDB line protocol to the URL in -forward-url:

  • VictoriaMetrics: -forward-url http://127.0.0.1:8428/influx/write
  • InfluxDB 2: -forward-url 'http://influxdb:8086/api/v2/write?org=home&bucket=health&precision=ns' with -forward-token-file
  • InfluxDB 1.x: -forward-url 'http://influxdb:8086/write?db=health'
  • Prometheus: through Telegraf's HTTP listener, which accepts line protocol

See Grafana for the details.

docs.title: Can I query Apple Health data with DuckDB?
docs.text:
Yes. The server keeps every record in Parquet files, one folder per type and month, and publishes SQL views for them. Start DuckDB in the archive folder with the views and query:

SELECT date_trunc('day', start) AS day, avg(value) AS resting_hr
FROM samples
WHERE type = 'HKQuantityTypeIdentifierRestingHeartRate'
GROUP BY day ORDER BY day DESC LIMIT 7;

Data model & querying explains the views. The query API runs the same SQL over HTTP for notebooks and dashboards.

docs.title: Is there a free alternative to Health Auto Export?
docs.text: Health Relay is free and open source (MIT), with every feature included. Both apps send Apple Health data off the iPhone automatically. Health Relay sends it to its own server program, which you run: the server stores everything losslessly in Parquet (routes, ECG voltages, heartbeat series, deletions), and forwards numbers to VictoriaMetrics or InfluxDB. Health Auto Export offers its automations as Premium features, and exports CSV, JSON or GPX to destinations such as REST APIs, MQTT, Home Assistant and cloud drives.

docs.title: How is this different from the Health app's "Export All Health Data"?
docs.text: The built-in export writes one zip with a large XML file, by hand, each time you want new data. Health Relay syncs on its own in the background, a little at a time, deletions included, and stores the data by type, ready to query.

docs.title: Which data does it sync?
docs.text: Everything HealthKit offers on the iPhone, over 200 types: heart rate, HRV, resting heart rate, sleep stages, steps, VO2 max, blood oxygen, workouts with their GPS routes, ECGs, blood pressure, cycle tracking, medications and more. Apple Watch data reaches it through the iPhone's Health app. Data model & querying has the full list.

docs.title: Where does my data go?
docs.text: From your iPhone to the server you pair the app with, and from there wherever you send it, such as Grafana or a backup. The privacy policy and Security & privacy describe each step.

docs.title: Does the server have to be on the internet?
docs.text: The iPhone syncs whenever it can reach the server. A server on your home network gets data while you are home; Tailscale or another VPN extends that to anywhere. See Networking & HTTPS.

docs.title: Does it work on Android or with Health Connect?
docs.text: Health Relay reads Apple Health on the iPhone. The server's upload API is documented in the server README, so another app could send data to it.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: These are the words this guide uses. Each one names one thing, and every page uses the same word for it.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
The healthkit-relay program, running on a computer you keep on: a home server, a NAS, a Raspberry Pi, a Mac or a small rented server (a VPS, virtual private server). Your iPhone sends its Health data to the server, and the server keeps it in the archive.

Example: in the Quick start, docker compose up -d starts the server in Docker. The setup guides show the other ways to run it.

docs.title: Server address
docs.text:
The address your iPhone uses to reach the server. You set it with the -public-url flag, or the HKR_PUBLIC_URL setting, and the server puts it in every setup code.

Examples:

  • http://192.168.1.10:8080: the server on your home Wi-Fi, at the IP address 192.168.1.10, port 8080.
  • https://health.example.ts.net: the server over Tailscale, with HTTPS (see Networking & HTTPS).

docs.title: Setup page
docs.text:
The server's web page for pairing iPhones and creating read tokens. Its address is the server address followed by /setup. You sign in to it with the admin token.

Example: http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup, opened in a browser on a computer at home.

docs.title: Admin token
docs.text:
The password of your server. The server makes it on its first start and prints it once, in its log. It signs in to the setup page and manages tokens. Save it in a password manager. healthkit-relay admin reset makes a new one, and the old one stops working at once.

Example: the first start of the server prints a line like this one in its log:

    Admin token: BBvGW16otZlTAfIc7RbrNmMVd7PXBVU8skBFvHZhO_4

docs.title: Setup code
docs.text:
A one-time code that pairs one iPhone. The setup page shows it as a QR code, and healthkit-relay pair prints one in the terminal. A setup code works once and expires after 15 minutes.

Example: the code PONKKR6RFXEX5WUCJQI6EBNX. The QR code holds it as a link that opens the app, with the server address:

healthrelay://pair?code=PONKKR6RFXEX5WUCJQI6EBNX&server=http%3A%2F%2F192.168.1.10%3A8080

docs.title: Paired device
docs.text:
An iPhone that has used a setup code. Each paired device gets a token of its own, kept in the iPhone's Keychain, that uploads its Health data and does nothing else. The setup page lists paired devices under Paired devices. Revoking one stops it at once.

Example: healthkit-relay devices lists a paired device as 3f9a1c2e iPhone iPhone16,1 upload 2026-10-19 14:02 just now.

docs.title: Read token
docs.text:
A token that lets a dashboard, a script or an AI agent read your data through the query API, and do nothing else. You create one on the setup page under Read tokens, or with healthkit-relay token create -name grafana. The server shows it once.

Example: a read token named grafana, pasted into Grafana as Authorization: Bearer ifg0UV7nzyvZmNFG944ioBl-Gy1ubAxxUThIJ52hV9I.

docs.title: Archive
docs.text:
The folder where the server keeps your data, as Parquet files (a file format for tables that DuckDB, Python and many other tools read). You set it with -archive-dir. It also holds the server's own files: admin.json, devices.json and codes.json. Back it up (see Backups).

Examples: ./data next to docker-compose.yml with Docker Compose; /var/lib/healthkit-relay with systemd or NixOS. See Data model & querying for what is inside.

docs.title: Query API
docs.text:
The read-only web API (application programming interface: a set of addresses that programs call to get data) under /v1/types. It answers with your data as JSON, for dashboards, scripts and AI agents. It is described at /openapi.json and shown as a web page at /docs. You turn it on with -query-duckdb; it takes a read token. See Query API.

Example: your steps per day in October 2026, in Toronto time, with the read token in $TOKEN:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "http://192.168.1.10:8080/v1/types/HKQuantityTypeIdentifierStepCount/aggregates?tz=America/Toronto&start=2026-10-01&end=2026-11-01"

docs.title: Grafana
docs.text:
Grafana draws dashboards: charts of your heart rate, steps, sleep and workouts over time. It reads them from a time-series database, a database for numbers over time. The server fills that database: with -forward-url set, it sends each new number it stores, such as a heart rate reading, to the database as well.

VictoriaMetrics is the easiest database to pair with Grafana; InfluxDB works too. Grafana shows the numbers. For the rest of the archive (routes, ECGs, sleep sessions as rows), use DuckDB or the query API.

docs.title: With Docker Compose
docs.text:
The Compose file has VictoriaMetrics and Grafana ready, with Grafana already connected to VictoriaMetrics. Run these in the folder with docker-compose.yml:

  1. Tell the server to forward numbers to VictoriaMetrics:

    echo HKR_FORWARD_URL=http://victoriametrics:8428/influx/write >> .env

  2. Start the server, VictoriaMetrics and Grafana:

    docker compose --profile metrics up -d

    docker compose --profile metrics ps lists relay, victoriametrics and grafana, each with a status of Up.

  3. Check that the server forwards:

    docker compose logs relay | grep forwarding

    It shows forwarding numeric samples to http://victoriametrics:8428/influx/write.

  4. In the app, tap Sync Now. New data goes to VictoriaMetrics as it arrives.

  5. Open Grafana on port 3000 of the server, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:3000. Sign in with the user admin and the password admin; Grafana then asks you to choose a new password.
  6. Open Explore from the menu. The data source is VictoriaMetrics. Type healthkit_heart_rate in the query box and click Run query. A chart of your heart rate appears.

VictoriaMetrics keeps data for 100 years in this Compose file (-retentionPeriod=100y).

The server forwards the numbers it stores from now on. To send the history it already holds, open the app's Advanced screen (the gear) and tap Erase Server Data and Start Over: the iPhone uploads its whole history again, and the server forwards all of it. See Erasing for what that deletes first.

docs.title: With VictoriaMetrics on your server
docs.text:
1. Install and start VictoriaMetrics, with a long retention, e.g. victoria-metrics -retentionPeriod=100y. Its default keeps one month, and the first sync sends your entire history, so a month would drop most of it. On NixOS, see VictoriaMetrics.

  2. Start the server with:

    -forward-url http://127.0.0.1:8428/influx/write

    (HKR_FORWARD_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8428/influx/write in /etc/healthkit-relay/env, or forwardUrl on NixOS). The server's log shows forwarding numeric samples to ....

  3. In Grafana, open Connections › Data sources, add a Prometheus data source with the URL http://127.0.0.1:8428 (VictoriaMetrics answers Prometheus queries), and click Save & test. Grafana reports that it queried the data source successfully.

  4. Open Explore, pick that data source, and run healthkit_heart_rate.

The archive keeps everything, whatever the retention of the time-series database.

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
VictoriaMetrics names each series <measurement>_<field>, so heart rate becomes healthkit_heart_rate, with the labels source (e.g. Apple Watch) and unit (e.g. count/min). Field names are listed in Metrics forwarding. Example queries, in PromQL (the Prometheus query language, which VictoriaMetrics's MetricsQL extends):

Panel PromQL / MetricsQL Heart rate healthkit_heart_rate Resting heart rate, daily avg_over_time(healthkit_resting_heart_rate[1d]) HRV (SDNN), 7-day average avg_over_time(healthkit_heart_rate_variability_sdnn[7d]) Steps per day, Apple Watch only sum_over_time(healthkit_step_count{source=~".*Watch.*"}[1d]) Sleep, hours per night sum by (value) (sum_over_time(healthkit_sleep_analysis_seconds{value=~"asleep.*"}[1d])) / 3600 VO2 max last_over_time(healthkit_vo2_max[30d]) Workout minutes per week sum_over_time(healthkit_workout_duration_seconds[7d]) / 60

Health samples come at irregular times (heart rate every few minutes, VO2 max every few days). Use the *_over_time functions with a window, and set the panel's Min interval to 1d for daily values.

docs.title: InfluxDB
docs.text:
InfluxDB 2:

-forward-url 'http://influxdb:8086/api/v2/write?org=home&bucket=health&precision=ns' \
-forward-token-file /path/to/influx-token

InfluxDB 1.x: -forward-url 'http://influxdb:8086/write?db=health'. Query the measurement healthkit, the field heart_rate, and so on.

docs.title: Prometheus
docs.text: Prometheus collects metrics by reading them from other programs, while the server sends them. Put VictoriaMetrics next to Prometheus (and add it to Grafana as a second Prometheus data source), or receive the lines with Telegraf's influxdb_listener input and expose them with its prometheus_client output.

docs.title: Monitoring the server itself
docs.text:
/metrics gives Prometheus metrics about the server itself: counts and timestamps. healthkit_relay_requests_total{result}, healthkit_relay_records_total{outcome}, healthkit_relay_archive_records, healthkit_relay_staged_records, healthkit_relay_last_success_timestamp_seconds{job="flush"|"compaction"}, healthkit_relay_maintenance_errors_total{job}, healthkit_relay_devices, healthkit_relay_forward_errors_total, healthkit_relay_admin_token_uploads_total, healthkit_relay_last_upload_timestamp_seconds and healthkit_relay_batches_total{trigger} (batches by what started the sync: foreground, observer, refresh, unlock, retry, or unknown for apps before 0.6.1). Collect them with VictoriaMetrics or Prometheus.

Useful alerts:

  • the hourly flush has not succeeded for two hours, or the nightly compaction for a day and a half:

    time() - healthkit_relay_last_success_timestamp_seconds{job="flush"} > 7200
time() - healthkit_relay_last_success_timestamp_seconds{job="compaction"} > 129600

  • no upload for a day, which usually means the phone could not reach the server, or background syncing is paused:

    time() - healthkit_relay_last_upload_timestamp_seconds > 86400

Whether the phone syncs in the background at all shows in:

sum by (trigger) (increase(healthkit_relay_batches_total{trigger!~"foreground|unknown"}[1d]))

docs.title: Networking & HTTPS
docs.text:
Your iPhone reaches the server at the server address, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080 at home or https://health.example.ts.net from anywhere. It needs the server only when it syncs: the app keeps what it has not sent yet and sends it at the next sync that reaches the server. Choose one of three setups:

Syncs from HTTPS Ports opened on your router Effort Tailscale anywhere yes, automatic none low Reverse proxy (Caddy) anywhere yes, automatic 443 medium Home network only your home Wi-Fi no none lowest

Keep plain HTTP inside your home network

Over plain HTTP, tokens and health data cross the network as readable text. The app uses plain HTTP only with local addresses. Put any server the internet can reach behind HTTPS.

docs.title: Tailscale (recommended)
docs.text:
Tailscale puts the server and your iPhone on a private network of your own, a tailnet, that works from anywhere. tailscale serve gives the server an HTTPS address with a real certificate, e.g. https://health.example.ts.net. The free plan is enough.

  1. Install Tailscale on the computer running the server and on the iPhone, and sign in to the same account on both.
  2. In the Tailscale admin console, open the DNS page and enable MagicDNS and HTTPS Certificates.

  3. On the server's computer, publish the server inside your tailnet:

    sudo tailscale serve --bg --https=443 http://127.0.0.1:8080
tailscale serve status

    If the first command prints a link to enable Serve, open it and approve. The second prints the HTTPS address, e.g. https://health.example.ts.net.

  4. Set the server address to it and restart the server:

    Setup Setting Docker Compose HKR_PUBLIC_URL=https://health.example.ts.net in .env, then docker compose up -d systemd HKR_PUBLIC_URL=https://health.example.ts.net in /etc/healthkit-relay/env, then systemctl restart healthkit-relay NixOS publicUrl = "https://health.example.ts.net";, then nixos-rebuild switch

    The server can stay on -listen 127.0.0.1:8080: tailscale serve reaches it there.

  5. Pair from https://health.example.ts.net/setup (see Pairing an iPhone). An iPhone you already paired with another address needs a new setup code.

The iPhone syncs whenever the Tailscale app is connected. In the Tailscale iOS app, turn on VPN On Demand, so the iPhone stays on your tailnet for background syncs.

With Docker, run Tailscale on the host as above, or add a Tailscale sidecar container that shares the network namespace of the server's container.

When the server can run the tailscale command and no server address is set, the setup page offers the ts.net address under Server address in the code.

Serve, not Funnel

tailscale funnel publishes a service on the public internet. Keep the server inside your tailnet with tailscale serve.

docs.title: Reverse proxy with Caddy
docs.text:
A reverse proxy is a web server that receives HTTPS requests and passes them to the server. If the server's computer has a public domain name, e.g. health.example.com, Caddy gets and renews a Let's Encrypt certificate for it by itself.

/etc/caddy/Caddyfile
health.example.com {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080
    request_body {
        max_size 32MB
    }
}

Then run the server with:

-listen 127.0.0.1:8080 -public-url https://health.example.com
  • Keep -setup-from private, the default. The setup page and pairing then answer only clients on private networks: pair from home, or over a VPN. With a proxy on the same computer, the server reads the client's address from the last entry of X-Forwarded-For.
  • The app uses /v1/pair, /v1/samples, /v1/status and /v1/data. The setup page is under /setup, and the query API under /v1/types, with /openapi.json and /docs. To publish less, allow only the paths you use at the proxy.
  • nginx, Traefik and HAProxy work the same way: proxy to 127.0.0.1:8080, pass X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Host, and allow request bodies of 32 MB.

docs.title: Home network only
docs.text:
The simplest setup: plain HTTP on your home network, with nothing published on the internet. The iPhone syncs when it is on your home Wi-Fi.

  1. Make the server listen on your network: -listen 0.0.0.0:8080. The Docker image already does.
  2. Give the server's computer a fixed address, with a DHCP reservation in your router.
  3. Set the server address to it, e.g. -public-url http://192.168.1.10:8080.
  4. Pair from http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup.

Notes:

  • The app uses plain HTTP with local addresses: IP addresses and .local names. Use the IP address, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080, or http://<hostname>.local:8080.
  • iOS asks once for Local Network access: allow it, so the app can reach the server. To change it later: Settings › Privacy & Security › Local Network › Health Relay.
  • Anyone on the same network can read traffic over plain HTTP. On a shared network, use Tailscale.
  • Background syncs happen while the iPhone is at home. Data from a trip reaches the server when you are back: the app keeps it until then.

docs.title: Pairing an iPhone
docs.text: Pairing connects the Health Relay app to your server. You show the iPhone a setup code, a one-time code that the setup page shows as a QR code. The app trades it for a token of its own, and the iPhone becomes a paired device: its token uploads its Health data and does nothing else. The admin token stays with you, and you can revoke each paired device on its own. The glossary defines each of these words.

docs.title: From the setup page
docs.text:
1. On a computer, open the setup page: your server address followed by /setup, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup on your home network or https://health.example.ts.net/setup with Tailscale. Enter the admin token and click Sign in. The sign-in lasts one hour.
  2. The page shows Pair your iPhone, a QR code and Waiting for your iPhone, with the time the code expires. If it also shows Server address in the code, click the address your iPhone reaches.
  3. On the iPhone, open the Camera, point it at the QR code and tap Open in Health Relay.
  4. The app asks whether to connect to your server: tap Connect. If iOS asks to find devices on your local network, tap Allow.
  5. The setup page shows iPhone paired and your iPhone's name. A few seconds later it shows a new code and lists your iPhone under Paired devices.
  6. In the app, tap Continue under Allow Health access. Health asks what Health Relay may read: turn on every category, then tap Allow. (On iOS 27, tap Select All, then All Recorded Data.)

To pair without a second screen, the setup page also shows a link with the code and a copy button. Send the link to the iPhone, e.g. by message to yourself, and open it there: the page shows an Open in Health Relay button. Tap it, then continue at step 4.

docs.title: The first sync
docs.text:
The first sync sends your whole Health history. With years of Apple Watch data it takes a while: keep the app open until it is done.

  • The app shows Syncing, then Up to date and when it last synced, e.g. Synced 2 minutes ago.
  • Records on server counts the records the server holds.
  • The card with your server address shows Connected as and your iPhone's name.

After that, Health Relay syncs in the background several times a day; open the app to sync right away. iPhone keeps Health data locked while the phone is locked, so background syncs happen after you unlock it. Low Power Mode, and swiping the app away in the app switcher, hold them back until you open the app. Sync Now, or pulling down on the main screen, syncs at once; on iOS 26 and later, a long sync started this way goes on when you leave the app, and iOS shows its progress in a Live Activity, where you can also stop it.

docs.title: From the terminal
docs.text:
On the server, pair prints a setup code as a QR code in the terminal, with the setup page's link for the same code:

docker compose exec relay healthkit-relay pair                    # Docker Compose
sudo healthkit-relay-ctl pair                                     # NixOS
sudo healthkit-relay pair -archive-dir /var/lib/healthkit-relay \
  -public-url http://192.168.1.10:8080                            # systemd
healthkit-relay pair -archive-dir ./data \
  -public-url http://192.168.1.10:8080                            # a server you run yourself

Scan the QR code with the iPhone's Camera, then continue at step 3 above.

The commands (pair, devices, revoke, token create, admin reset) change the files in the archive (-archive-dir or HKR_ARCHIVE_DIR), with the server running. The server rereads the files when they change. Run the commands as the server's user or as root. They take the server's flags and HKR_ variables: -public-url sets the server address in the code.

To send the code's link to your iPhone by message or email, make the code last longer, up to 24h:

healthkit-relay pair -archive-dir ./data -public-url http://192.168.1.10:8080 -valid 2h

docs.title: Managing devices
docs.text:
The setup page lists your paired devices under Paired devices, each with a Revoke button. From the terminal:

healthkit-relay devices -archive-dir ./data
healthkit-relay revoke  -archive-dir ./data 3f9a1c2e

devices prints one line per paired device and read token, e.g.:

ID        NAME    MODEL       SCOPE   CREATED           LAST SEEN
3f9a1c2e  iPhone  iPhone16,1  upload  2026-10-19 14:02  5 min ago

Revoking takes effect at once. At its next sync, the app shows Disconnected and asks you to scan a new setup code. Pairing the same iPhone again gives it a new token, and its old token stops working.

docs.title: How setup codes work
docs.text:
• A setup code is 120 random bits, written as 24 letters and digits, e.g. PONKKR6RFXEX5WUCJQI6EBNX. It works once and expires after 15 minutes, or after the time pair -valid sets, up to a day. The server keeps the codes' SHA-256 hashes in codes.json in the archive, so a code still works after a restart, until it expires.
  • The QR code holds a link that opens the app, with the code and the server address: healthrelay://pair?code=PONKKR6RFXEX5WUCJQI6EBNX&server=http%3A%2F%2F192.168.1.10%3A8080.
  • The app trades the code for its own token, 256 random bits. The server keeps only the token's SHA-256 hash, with the iPhone's name and model.
  • By default, the setup page and pairing answer only private networks (-setup-from private): the server's own computer, your home network (addresses such as 192.168.1.25) and Tailscale. -setup-from off turns the setup page off; the terminal commands keep working.
  • A code holds an address the iPhone can reach: a LAN or Tailscale address, a tailscale serve name, or -public-url. Loopback (127.0.0.1) and link-local addresses stay out. When the server finds no such address, the setup page shows Set the server address, with how to set -public-url.

docs.title: Manual setup
docs.text:
In the app, Enter Server Details Instead takes the server address and the admin token. The app trades the admin token for a token of its own straight away, and keeps only that one.

An app set up by hand with an earlier version may still upload with the admin token (the server token of earlier versions). This release accepts it, logs a warning at most once an hour and counts it in healthkit_relay_admin_token_uploads_total on /metrics. Pair that iPhone again from the setup page.

docs.title: Leaving
docs.text:
In the app, open Advanced (the gear icon):

  • Disconnect forgets the server on the iPhone. The data on the server stays there.
  • Erase Server Data and Start Over deletes everything this iPhone uploaded, for good, then uploads it all again.

To delete one iPhone's data and keep it deleted, revoke the paired device, then erase its data with the admin token and the device's ID from devices:

curl -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer <admin token>" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/data?confirm=erase&device=3f9a1c2e"

To delete everything, stop the server and delete the archive. Read Backups before you do either.

docs.title: Privacy policy
docs.text:
Effective October 25, 2026. Applies to the Health Relay app for iPhone and to the healthkit-relay server software.

Health Relay is published by François Leblanc ("we"). It copies your Apple Health data to a server that you set up and run, such as the healthkit-relay program on a computer at home, a NAS or a cloud server you rent. We do not run that server, and we receive none of your data.

docs.title: Data the app reads
docs.text:
With your permission, given in Apple Health's own permission sheet, the app reads the Health data types you allow, for example:

  • activity: steps, distance, flights climbed, active and resting energy, exercise and stand time, workouts with their routes;
  • heart: heart rate, heart rate variability, resting and walking heart rate, ECG recordings, irregular rhythm notifications, blood oxygen;
  • body measurements and vital signs: weight, height, body fat, temperature, blood pressure, respiratory rate;
  • sleep, mindfulness and State of Mind;
  • nutrition, hydration, medications you log in Health, and cycle tracking;
  • hearing, vision prescriptions, and your characteristics (date of birth, biological sex, blood type).

You pick the types in Apple Health's sheet, and can change your choice at any time in Settings › Health › Data Access & Devices › Health Relay. The app only reads: it leaves your Health data as it is. The App Store version of the app reads no clinical health records.

docs.title: Where the data goes
docs.text:
• To your server only. The app sends the data it reads to the server address you set up, over HTTPS, or over plain HTTP to an address on your own local network if you choose one (others on that network can then read it). The server keeps it in files on your own computer.
  • Kept between you and your server. The app connects to your server and to nothing else; its code is all its own, without analytics, advertising, tracking or crash-reporting libraries. We, and any third party, have no access to your data, and it is used for no advertising, marketing or data mining.
  • On your iPhone. While a batch waits to be sent, the app keeps it in its own storage, protected by iOS until you first unlock the iPhone, and left out of iCloud and computer backups. Each batch is deleted once sent. The server address and the app's token are in the iPhone's Keychain, for this device only.
  • Diagnostic log. The app keeps a small log of sync steps and counts on the iPhone (no Health values). It leaves the iPhone only if you share it yourself from Advanced › Share Diagnostic Log.

In App Store terms, the app collects no data: nothing leaves your iPhone except to the server you set up.

docs.title: The demo server
docs.text: So that Apple's App Review can try the app without a server of its own, we run a demonstration server, reachable with a setup code given to App Review. It stores nothing about the people who use it: it checks each batch it receives, answers it and drops it, keeping only the total number of records received in the last hour, all devices together. Devices paired with it get a signed token that the server checks without keeping a list of devices, names or addresses. It runs on Cloudflare Workers, at health-relay-demo.leblancfg.com, with request logs turned off; Cloudflare carries its traffic, as a hosting provider does. It is not part of the app's normal use.

docs.title: Keeping and deleting your data
docs.text:
Your server keeps your data for as long as you keep it there. You control it completely:

  • Delete it from your server: in the app, Advanced › Erase Server Data and Disconnect stops syncing, then has your server permanently delete everything your iPhone sent and revoke its token. (Erase Server Data and Start Over deletes it too, then sends your Health data again from the start.) This deletes the server's archive; copies you made from it yourself, such as backups or numbers forwarded to a metrics database, follow their own settings. You can also delete the server's files yourself.
  • Stop syncing: Advanced › Disconnect in the app, or turn off Health Relay's access in the Health settings above.
  • Remove the app: deleting the app removes its pending batches, sync positions and log from your iPhone. iOS keeps the app's Keychain items (server address and token); a new install of Health Relay clears them on its first start. To make that token useless right away, revoke this iPhone on your server's setup page.

The app works without an account: you set it up with your own server's setup code, and everything about you stays on your iPhone and your server.

docs.title: Children
docs.text: The app is not directed at children and collects no data from anyone.

docs.title: Changes
docs.text: If this policy changes, the new version is posted on this page with a new effective date.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: Questions about privacy: healthrelay@leblancfg.com.

docs.title: Query API
docs.text:
The query API lets a program read your health data from the server: a Grafana dashboard, a script, or an AI agent. It answers questions such as "steps per day last week", "average heart rate per hour" or "minutes of deep sleep per night". It reads the archive, the folder where the server keeps your data, and it only reads: no request changes anything.

An API (application programming interface) is a set of web addresses that answer programs instead of people. Each answer is JSON, a text format that programs read easily. The query API is described by an OpenAPI 3.1 document at /openapi.json and shown as a page you can try out at /docs, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080/docs.

To use it you need:

  • the server address, the address the iPhone uses to reach the server, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080;
  • a read token: a password for one program, that reads your data through the query API and does nothing else. You create one for each program, e.g. one named grafana.

The query API starts when the server has the -query-duckdb setting; until then, its addresses answer 404.

docs.title: Types and kinds
docs.text:
A type is one specific HealthKit measurement, named by HealthKit's identifier: HKQuantityTypeIdentifierStepCount, HKQuantityTypeIdentifierHeartRate, HKCategoryTypeIdentifierSleepAnalysis. A kind is the shape of a type's data. Each type has one kind: HKQuantityTypeIdentifierStepCount is a type of kind quantity.

Kind Shape Example quantity a number with a unit steps: 12027 count on 2026-10-15; heart rate: 67 count/min at 09:04 category a labelled interval sleep: asleepDeep from 01:10 to 01:40; stand hours: stood from 14:00 to 15:00 workout, heartbeat_series, electrocardiogram, audiogram, correlation, ... a record with fields of its own a run with its duration, energy and distance; an ECG with its classification

Quantity and category types have aggregates (totals and averages per day or hour). For the other kinds, read the samples with raw=true. GET /v1/types lists every type with its kind; GET /v1/types?kind=category lists the types of one kind.

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
The server runs each query with DuckDB, a database program that reads the archive's Parquet files. You install the duckdb program next to the server, then tell the server where it is.

  1. Install duckdb, version 1.2 or newer (tested with 1.5), on the computer that runs the server:

    brew install duckdb          # macOS

    On Linux, download the duckdb command-line program for your system from duckdb.org and copy it to /usr/local/bin. Check it:

    duckdb --version

    It prints a version such as v1.5.0.

  2. Give the server the path of duckdb with -query-duckdb (or HKR_QUERY_DUCKDB):

    • Linux with systemd: add HKR_QUERY_DUCKDB=/usr/local/bin/duckdb to /etc/healthkit-relay/env, then sudo systemctl restart healthkit-relay.
    • macOS: add <string>-query-duckdb</string><string>/opt/homebrew/bin/duckdb</string> (the path which duckdb prints) to the ProgramArguments of the launchd agent (see macOS), run launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/io.github.healthkit-relay, then the launchctl bootstrap command from that page again.
    • NixOS: services.healthkit-relay.extraFlags = [ "-query-duckdb" "${pkgs.duckdb}/bin/duckdb" ];, then sudo nixos-rebuild switch.

    • From a terminal:

      healthkit-relay -archive-dir /var/lib/healthkit-relay -query-duckdb /usr/local/bin/duckdb

    The Docker image holds the server program alone. To use the query API, run the server from one of the setups above.

  3. Read the server's log. It shows a line like this one:

    query API on: /usr/local/bin/duckdb reads /var/lib/healthkit-relay/parquet; /docs, /openapi.json

    A second line with the test query failed means duckdb could not read the archive: the line ends with DuckDB's reason.

  4. Open the /docs page in a browser, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080/docs. It shows Health Relay query API, with every endpoint.

Samples reach the Parquet files at the hourly flush. Samples the server received in the last hour appear in the query API after the next flush.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Flag Default -query-duckdb (empty: the query API is off) the duckdb program -query-archive-dir -archive-dir the archive whose parquet/ is read, e.g. a replica or a restored backup -query-timeout 30s longest a query may run, waiting for a free slot included; DuckDB is stopped at the deadline -query-max-rows 50000 most rows one query may return -query-memory-limit 512MB DuckDB memory_limit per query; a query needing more fails (it never spills to disk) -query-threads 2 DuckDB threads per query -query-concurrency 2 queries that may run at once; the others wait, up to -query-timeout, then get 503

Each flag has an environment variable: HKR_ and the name in capitals, with _ for - (HKR_QUERY_TIMEOUT=60s).

docs.title: Get a read token
docs.text:
You create read tokens on the server's setup page, its /setup page. You sign in to it with the admin token, the password of your server, which the server printed on its first start (see Troubleshooting if you do not have it). The /docs page links to the right place.

  1. On a computer on your home network (or your Tailscale network), open the setup page at its read tokens section, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup#read-tokens. The page asks for the Admin token.
  2. Paste the admin token and click Sign in. The page shows Read tokens, below Pair your iPhone and Paired devices.
  3. Under Read tokens, type a name that says what the token is for, e.g. grafana, in the box that says Name, e.g. grafana. Click Create.
  4. The page shows Read token for grafana and the token, a line of 43 letters, digits, - and _. Click the copy button next to it. On a plain http:// address the button selects the token instead: press Ctrl+C (Cmd+C on a Mac).
  5. Paste the token into your password manager now. The server keeps only a fingerprint of it (its SHA-256) and shows it this once.
  6. Click Done. The Read tokens list now shows grafana, with the date it was created.

To stop a read token, click Revoke next to it under Read tokens. It stops working at once. Lost a token? Revoke it and create a new one.

docs.title: From a terminal
docs.text:
On the server, run token create as the server's user or as root, with the server's archive directory (see Commands):

healthkit-relay token create -archive-dir /var/lib/healthkit-relay -name grafana

q3vN8x2LkP0aTzR7mW5cYb1HdJ9eFgUs4oXiK6nVtQA
Created read token 4be1f07a (grafana). It is shown only this once; revoke it with: healthkit-relay revoke 4be1f07a

The first line is the token. With Docker Compose, run docker compose exec relay healthkit-relay token create -name grafana; on NixOS, sudo healthkit-relay-ctl token create -name grafana.

healthkit-relay devices lists paired devices and read tokens, with read in the SCOPE column for read tokens; healthkit-relay revoke 4be1f07a revokes one.

A program can also create a token with POST /v1/tokens and the admin token:

curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" -d '{"name": "grafana"}' \
  http://192.168.1.10:8080/v1/tokens

{"token":"q3vN8x2LkP0aTzR7mW5cYb1HdJ9eFgUs4oXiK6nVtQA","device":{"id":"4be1f07a","name":"grafana","created_at":"2026-10-19T14:02:11Z","last_seen_at":"2026-10-19T14:02:11Z","scope":"read"}}

docs.title: What each token may do
docs.text:
The server keeps the SHA-256 of every token in devices.json, in the archive directory: read tokens next to the paired devices, the iPhones that used a setup code. Each token has a scope, the list of what it may do.

Token Scope Query API Upload, status, erase Tokens, devices, pairing Admin token admin yes erase any paired device's data; uploads are deprecated yes Read token read yes no (403) no (401) A paired device's token upload no (403) yes, its own data no (401)

A paired device from a version before scopes has no scope in devices.json and counts as upload. /openapi.json and /docs are public: they describe the API and hold no data.

docs.title: Your first query
docs.text:
This sends one request with curl, a command-line program for web requests (installed on macOS and most Linux systems). Run it on any computer that reaches the server.

  1. Put the server address and your read token in two variables, so the next commands can use them:

    SERVER=http://192.168.1.10:8080
H="Authorization: Bearer q3vN8x2LkP0aTzR7mW5cYb1HdJ9eFgUs4oXiK6nVtQA"

  2. Ask which types have data:

    curl -H "$H" "$SERVER/v1/types?present=true"

    The answer starts with {"types":[{"identifier":"HKQuantityTypeIdentifierStepCount",.... It is one long line; the examples below spread it over several lines to read it.

  3. If it answers something else:

    Answer Meaning What to do {"error":"unauthorized"} the server does not know this token check that you pasted the whole token; create a new one if it was revoked another {"error": ...} the server refused the request read the message: it says what to change, e.g. that a paired device's token cannot query 404 page not found the query API is off turn it on Failed to connect curl cannot reach the server check the address, as in Troubleshooting

  4. Ask for steps per day, with days in your time zone:

    curl -H "$H" "$SERVER/v1/types/HKQuantityTypeIdentifierStepCount/aggregates?tz=America/Toronto&start=2026-10-15&end=2026-10-17"

    The answer has one bucket per day, with "sum": 12027 and the like. More examples follow.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
All GET, with Authorization: Bearer <token>.

Path /v1/types every HealthKit type, with kind, unit, aggregation style, category labels and what the archive holds (count, first and last sample); ?present=true keeps the types with data, ?kind=category the types of one kind /v1/types/{type} one type /v1/types/{type}/samples its samples in [start, end), page by page (limit, cursor, order, raw) /v1/types/{type}/aggregates per day or hour (interval), in a time zone (tz)

{type} is a HealthKit identifier such as HKQuantityTypeIdentifierStepCount. In the OpenAPI document it is a string that starts with HK (the pattern ^HK[A-Za-z]+Type[A-Za-z0-9]*$), with examples; GET /v1/types lists the valid values, over 200 of them, from the iOS SDK the app is built with. An unknown type answers 400 with the closest names:

curl -H "$H" "$SERVER/v1/types/HKQuantityTypeIdentifierSteps"

{"error":"unknown type HKQuantityTypeIdentifierSteps; did you mean HKQuantityTypeIdentifierStepCount?"}

kind takes one of the kinds the OpenAPI document lists (quantity, category, workout, ...).

Times are RFC 3339 timestamps with an offset, e.g. 2026-10-17T09:00:00-04:00. start and end also take a date, e.g. 2026-10-17, meaning midnight in tz. tz is a time zone name such as America/Toronto; the default is UTC.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Every error is JSON with an error message, e.g. {"error":"tz \"Mars/Olympus\" is not in the time zone database"}.

Status When 400 a parameter is wrong: an unknown type, a bad date, a range over the limit 401 no token, or a token the server does not know 403 a paired device's token 422 the answer would be too large: ask for fewer rows or a shorter range 503 too many queries at once: try again after the Retry-After seconds 504 the query took longer than -query-timeout: ask for a shorter range

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
These use the SERVER and H variables from Your first query.

Which types have data, of one kind:

curl -H "$H" "$SERVER/v1/types?present=true&kind=category"

{"types": [
  {"identifier": "HKCategoryTypeIdentifierAppleStandHour", "kind": "category",
   "display_name": "Apple Stand Hour", "value_enum": "HKCategoryValueAppleStandHour",
   "values": [{"value": 0, "label": "stood"}, {"value": 1, "label": "idle"}], "aggregates": true,
   "data": {"samples": 41632, "first_start": "2021-06-30T00:00:00Z", "last_start": "2026-10-18T19:00:00Z"}},
  ...
]}

    {"value": 3, "label": "asleepCore", "samples": 14, "seconds": 13500, "sources": ["Apple Watch"]},

{"type": "HKQuantityTypeIdentifierHeartRate", "start": "2026-10-17T09:00:00-04:00", ..., "count": 2,

  ...
