docs.title: Aggregates
docs.text:
What a bucket holds depends on the type:

  • Cumulative quantities (steps, distances, energy, exercise minutes): sum. A sample spanning two buckets is split in proportion to the time in each.
  • Discrete quantities (heart rate, HRV, body mass...): avg, min, max of the samples starting in the bucket. Sound exposure averages as energy (10·log10(mean(10^(dB/10)))), as Apple does. Temporally weighted types (heart rate) are averaged per sample, each sample counting once whatever its duration.
  • Categories (sleep, stand hours, symptoms...): per value, the samples and the seconds they cover inside the bucket. A night's sleep is cut at local midnight: a day bucket holds the part of each night after its midnight. Use interval=hour, or the samples, to cut nights elsewhere.

One request covers at most 366 days or 744 hours. Days are local calendar days of tz (23 or 25 hours across a daylight saving time change).

docs.title: Counting each moment once (dedup)
docs.text:
An Apple Watch and an iPhone carried together both count steps, distance and energy; other apps may write the same thing again. Summing every sample counts the same steps twice. With dedup=priority, the default, sources are ranked Apple Watch, then iPhone, then any other app or device (from the sample's hardware model, e.g. Watch6,14), and a sample counts only for the part of its time that no sample of a higher-ranked source covers. For categories, a sample is covered only by a sample of the same value: the watch's sleep stages leave the phone's in bed whole. Apple Health merges sources the same way with its default source order: the watch wins where both measured, and the phone fills the time the watch was off the wrist.

Checked against the daily totals Apple's Activity app computes (the activity summaries in the archive), over 365 days of one person's data with two iPhones and a watch:

Rule Active energy, mean daily error Exercise minutes, mean daily error priority (default) 6.5 kcal (0.8%) 1.3 min (2.3%) one source per hour (watch first) 4.7 kcal 4.7 min (drops phone-only minutes) largest source per hour 17.6 kcal 1.2 min none (sum everything) 36.9 kcal (4.7%) 10.4 min (19%)

dedup=none sums every sample, for when you want each source's count.

docs.title: How queries run
docs.text:
Each query is a fresh duckdb process, in memory, reading the archive through the views in server/sql/views.sql, which hide samples deleted in Apple Health. Before the query, the server sets:

  • enable_external_access = false, with allowed_directories set to the archive's parquet/: DuckDB reads that folder and refuses every other file, the network and getenv;
  • autoinstall_known_extensions = false, autoload_known_extensions = false;
  • memory_limit, threads, temp_directory = '' (everything stays in memory), preserve_insertion_order = false;
  • lock_configuration = true, which freezes those settings for the rest of the process.

DuckDB runs with an empty environment, as the server's user. Every query filters on the type and the months it needs (the archive's partitions), so DuckDB opens only those files. The values in each query come from the server: the type from its catalog, times it parsed, numbers it checked.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This page takes you, step by step, to an iPhone that syncs its Health data to your own server, on your home Wi-Fi. It runs the server with Docker Compose; the setup guides show the other ways. New to the words server address, setup page or admin token? The glossary explains each one with an example.

You need:

  • A computer that stays on, running Linux or macOS, with Docker. This computer runs the server. To install Docker, follow Docker Engine on Linux or Docker Desktop on a Mac. Check it with docker compose version: it prints Docker Compose version v2....
  • An iPhone on the same Wi-Fi network as the server, with the Health Relay app from the App Store (in review in October 2026; until it is listed, build it yourself). (To build the app yourself instead: a Mac with Xcode 16 or newer and a paid Apple Developer Program membership, see step 3.)

docs.title: 1. Find the server address
docs.text:
The server address is the address your iPhone uses to reach the server. On your home network it is the IP address of the computer that runs the server, followed by the port 8080.

On that computer, run:

hostname -I               # Linux: the first address, e.g. 192.168.1.10
ipconfig getifaddr en0    # macOS: e.g. 192.168.1.10

With 192.168.1.10, the server address is http://192.168.1.10:8080. Use your own address everywhere this page shows 192.168.1.10.

Keep the address fixed

Your router may give the computer a new address one day. To keep the same one, add a DHCP reservation for the computer in your router's settings.

docs.title: 2. Start the server
docs.text:
1. Make a folder for the server and go into it:

    mkdir -p ~/healthkit-relay && cd ~/healthkit-relay

  2. Download the Compose file, which tells Docker how to run the server:

    curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leblancfg/healthkit-relay/main/docker-compose.yml

    ls now shows docker-compose.yml.

  3. Make the data folder, where the server keeps your data (the archive), and the .env file with your settings:

    mkdir -p data
printf 'HKR_USER=%s\nHKR_PUBLIC_URL=%s\n' "$(id -u):$(id -g)" http://192.168.1.10:8080 > .env
cat .env

    cat .env shows your user and group IDs and the server address, e.g.:

    HKR_USER=1000:1000
HKR_PUBLIC_URL=http://192.168.1.10:8080

  4. Start the server:

    docker compose up -d

    Docker downloads the server image and starts it. The last line ends with Started. If Docker answers permission denied, put sudo in front of each docker command on this page.

  5. Check that the server answers:

    curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz

    It prints ok.

  6. Read the admin token. The admin token is the password of your server: the server makes it on its first start and prints it once, in its log.

    docker compose logs relay

    Look for these two lines:

    relay-1  |     Admin token: BBvGW16otZlTAfIc7RbrNmMVd7PXBVU8skBFvHZhO_4
relay-1  |     Setup page:  http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup

    Save the admin token in a password manager. You sign in to the setup page with it. Lost it? docker compose exec relay healthkit-relay admin reset prints a new one.

More settings, updates and the optional dashboards are in Docker & Compose.

docs.title: 3. Install the iPhone app
docs.text:
Install Health Relay from the App Store on the iPhone (search for "Health Relay"). While the app is in review (October 2026), use "Build the app yourself instead" below. It opens on three steps, starting with Open your server's setup page: go on with step 4.

Build the app yourself instead

You build the app with Xcode on your Mac and install it on your iPhone from there. Apple requires a paid Apple Developer Program membership to sign apps that read Health data.

  1. Install XcodeGen, which writes the Xcode project, e.g. with Homebrew:

    brew install xcodegen

  2. Download the code and make your settings file:

    git clone https://github.com/leblancfg/healthkit-relay && cd healthkit-relay
cp ios/Config/Local.xcconfig.example ios/Config/Local.xcconfig

  3. Open ios/Config/Local.xcconfig in a text editor. Set your Team ID (on developer.apple.com, under Membership) and a bundle identifier of your own:

    HKR_BUNDLE_ID = com.yourname.healthkitrelay
HKR_TEAM_ID = ABCDE12345

  4. Make the Xcode project and open it:

    make ios-project && open ios/HealthKitRelay.xcodeproj

  5. Connect your iPhone to the Mac with a cable. In Xcode, choose your iPhone at the top of the window, then click Run (the triangle). The first time, turn on Developer Mode on the iPhone (Settings › Privacy & Security › Developer Mode) and trust the Mac.

Health Relay opens on the iPhone and shows three steps, starting with Open your server's setup page. More details: ios/README.md.

docs.title: 4. Pair the iPhone
docs.text:
Pairing connects the app to your server. The setup page shows a setup code: a QR code that pairs one iPhone, once, within 15 minutes.

  1. On a computer on your home network, open the setup page in a browser: http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup. The page shows Sign in and an Admin token field.
  2. Paste the admin token and click Sign in. The page shows Pair your iPhone, a QR code and Waiting for your iPhone.
  3. On the iPhone, open the Camera and point it at the QR code. Tap Open in Health Relay.
  4. The app asks whether to connect to your server. Tap Connect. If iOS asks to find devices on your local network, tap Allow.
  5. The setup page shows iPhone paired. A few seconds later it lists your iPhone under Paired devices: your iPhone is now a paired device.
  6. In the app, tap Continue under Allow Health access. Health asks what Health Relay may read: turn on every category, then tap Allow. (On iOS 27, tap Select All, then All Recorded Data.)

To pair from the terminal instead, run docker compose exec relay healthkit-relay pair in the server's folder: it prints the QR code. More in Pairing an iPhone.

docs.title: 5. Watch the first sync
docs.text:
The first sync sends your whole Health history. With years of Apple Watch data it takes a while: keep the app open until it is done.

  • The app shows Syncing, then Up to date and when it last synced, e.g. Synced 2 minutes ago. Under it, Records on server counts the records the server holds. The card with your server address shows Connected as and your iPhone's name.
  • The server log shows a line starting with batch for each batch it stores. To follow it, run docker compose logs -f relay, and press Ctrl+C to stop.

After the first sync, Health Relay syncs in the background several times a day; open the app to sync right away. iPhone keeps Health data locked while the phone is locked, so background syncs happen after you unlock it. Sync Now, at the bottom of the app, syncs at once.

docs.title: 6. Next steps
docs.text:
• Sync away from home: Networking & HTTPS. With Tailscale, the iPhone reaches the server over HTTPS from anywhere, and your router stays closed.
  • Ask questions of your data: Data model & querying, and the Query API for dashboards, scripts and AI agents.
  • Dashboards: Grafana. The Compose file's metrics profile adds VictoriaMetrics and Grafana next to the server; see Docker & Compose.
  • Set up Backups: the archive is the only copy of your history outside the iPhone.

docs.title: Security & privacy
docs.text: Health data is among the most sensitive data there is. With Health Relay, your data goes from your iPhone to your server, and only there. Words such as server address, admin token and read token are defined in the glossary.

docs.title: Where your data goes
docs.text:
• To your server. The app connects to one address: the server address you pair it with, e.g. https://health.example.ts.net. The server answers the app, and the programs you give a read token to.
  • To your metrics database, if you choose. With -forward-url set, the server also sends numbers (heart rate, steps...) to the address you give, e.g. your VictoriaMetrics.
  • Logs and metrics hold counts. The app's diagnostic log lists sync steps and counts. /healthz and /metrics give request counts and timestamps. Health values stay in the archive.
  • The code is open. The app and the server are built from this repository, and talk only to each other and to the addresses above.

docs.title: What the app can do
docs.text:
• Read Apple Health. It asks HealthKit for read access only; your Apple Health data stays as it is.
  • Keep its token on this iPhone. Its token and the server address are in the iPhone's Keychain, for this device only: iCloud Keychain and backups restored to another phone leave them out.
  • Wait for the unlock. While the phone is locked, iOS keeps HealthKit data encrypted; the app syncs after the next unlock.
  • Hand an upload to iOS. Each batch is written to a file in the app's own storage (readable after the first unlock since the iPhone started) and sent from there, so iOS can finish an upload after it suspends the app. The file is deleted once the upload is over.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Credential Where Can Admin token your password manager; the server keeps its SHA-256 in admin.json (mode 600) sign in to the setup page; pair, list and revoke paired devices; create read tokens; query; erase any paired device's data A paired device's token the iPhone's Keychain; the server keeps its SHA-256 in devices.json upload and read the server status, for one paired device; revocable Read token wherever the program keeps it, e.g. Grafana's settings; the server keeps its SHA-256 in devices.json read health data through the query API, and nothing else; revocable Setup code the QR code or its link; the server keeps its SHA-256 in codes.json pair one iPhone, once, within 15 minutes (up to 24 hours with pair -valid)

A SHA-256 is a fingerprint of a token: the server can check a token against it, and nobody can turn it back into the token.

The admin token is 256 random bits. The server generates it on its first start and prints it once to its log, with the setup page's address (docker compose logs relay, journalctl -u healthkit-relay). The log keeps that line, so whoever can read the server's logs can read the first admin token. To replace it with one that appears only in your terminal:

  1. Save the admin token from the log in your password manager, and check it signs in to the setup page.
  2. On the server, run healthkit-relay admin reset with the server's -archive-dir (with Docker Compose: docker compose exec relay healthkit-relay admin reset; on NixOS: sudo healthkit-relay-ctl admin reset).
  3. The terminal shows the new admin token. Save it in your password manager in place of the old one: the old one stops working at once.
  4. Open the setup page. Browsers signed in with the old token are signed out; sign in with the new one.

The setup page's sign-in is an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie that lasts an hour. Its responses are kept out of caches, send no referrer, and refuse to be shown in a frame.

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text:
Health Relay protects against:

  • Someone on the network path reading or altering data: use HTTPS (Tailscale or a reverse proxy). Plain HTTP is for trusted home networks only.
  • A client without a token reading, uploading or deleting data: every endpoint that reads or changes data needs a token, and each token does only what its scope allows.
  • A lost or sold phone: revoke it on the setup page; the admin token and the other paired devices keep working.
  • Pairing from outside: by default, the setup page and pairing answer private networks only (your home network, Tailscale).
  • Partial writes and retries: a batch is stored whole or not at all; a batch sent twice is stored once.

Your responsibility:

  • The server host. Anyone with root, or read access to the archive directory, can read everything. Use full-disk encryption, keep the host up to date, and restrict who logs in.
  • Backups. Encrypt them; see Backups.
  • Downstream tools. Grafana, the metrics database and anything that reads the Parquet files need their own access control.
  • The iPhone itself, and Apple Health.

docs.title: Hardening checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] HTTPS for anything beyond a trusted home network; never plain HTTP on the internet.
  • [ ] Admin token saved in a password manager, then replaced with healthkit-relay admin reset so the log no longer holds a working one.
  • [ ] -token-file from an earlier version removed: once the server has imported it into admin.json, delete the file and the flag.
  • [ ] -listen 127.0.0.1:8080 behind a reverse proxy or tailscale serve.
  • [ ] -setup-from private (the default), or off once your phones are paired.
  • [ ] The systemd hardening options from Linux binary + systemd.
  • [ ] Full-disk encryption on the server; encrypted off-site backups.
  • [ ] One read token per program, so you can revoke one alone.
  • [ ] Paired devices and read tokens you no longer use revoked on the setup page.

docs.title: Deleting your data
docs.text: Erase Server Data and Start Over, in the app's Advanced screen, permanently deletes everything that iPhone uploaded (Parquet rows, staged rows, de-duplication entries), then uploads its history again. To delete a paired device's data and keep it from uploading again, revoke it, then erase its data with the admin token (see Pairing). To delete everything, stop the server and delete the archive directory. Delete the data forwarded to a metrics database there too.

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text: Privately, through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting. See SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Not a medical device
docs.text: Health Relay copies data. It does not diagnose, treat or monitor any condition, has not been reviewed by any regulator, and is not a substitute for professional medical advice. Values may be incomplete, delayed or wrong. See DISCLAIMER.md.

docs.title: Help and support
docs.text: title: Help and support description: Get Health Relay working: setting up a server, pairing the iPhone, syncing, and how to reach us.

docs.title: Help and support
docs.text:
Health Relay copies your Apple Health data to a server you run yourself. Most questions are answered in these pages:

  • Setting up a server: Quick start (Docker, a single binary, NixOS, a NAS or a Raspberry Pi; about ten minutes).
  • Pairing the iPhone: Pairing an iPhone. On the server's setup page, scan the QR code with the iPhone's Camera, or in the app tap Enter Server Details Instead and type the server address and the setup code shown under the QR code.
  • Reaching the server from the iPhone, HTTPS: Networking & HTTPS.
  • Syncing: the app syncs in the background several times a day; open the app to sync right away. iPhone keeps Health data locked while the phone is locked, so background syncs happen after you unlock it. More in Troubleshooting.
  • Your data: Privacy policy and Security & privacy.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: Write to healthrelay@leblancfg.com. To help us help you, include the app's version (Advanced, at the bottom), the server's version (on its setup page), and, if a sync fails, the diagnostic log (Advanced › Share Diagnostic Log: sync steps and counts, without Health values). We answer within a few days.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Each problem below says what you see, why it happens, what to do, and how to check it worked. Words such as server address, setup page and admin token are defined in the glossary.

Start with the two logs:

  • the server's log: docker compose logs relay (Docker Compose), journalctl -u healthkit-relay (Linux and NixOS), or the terminal or log file it runs in;
  • the app's diagnostic log: in the app, tap the gear, then Share Diagnostic Log.

Both list steps and counts; health values stay in the archive. Remove your addresses before you share them.

docs.title: Where is the admin token?
docs.text:
What you see. The setup page asks for the Admin token, and you do not have it.

Why. The server prints the admin token once, in its log, on its very first start, and keeps only its fingerprint (admin.json).

What to do.

  1. Look in the log of the first start: docker compose logs relay | grep -i "admin token", or journalctl -u healthkit-relay | grep -i "admin token".

  2. If the log no longer has it, make a new one on the server:

    docker compose exec relay healthkit-relay admin reset        # Docker Compose
sudo healthkit-relay-ctl admin reset                         # NixOS
sudo healthkit-relay admin reset -archive-dir /var/lib/healthkit-relay   # Linux binary

    The terminal shows the new admin token. The old one stops working at once.

  3. Save it in your password manager.

Check. Paste it on the setup page and click Sign in: the page shows Pair your iPhone.

docs.title: A command says the archive directory "belongs to uid"
docs.text:
What you see. pair, devices, revoke, token create or admin reset stops with a message that the archive directory belongs to a uid (a user number), e.g. belongs to uid 61234.

Why. These commands change the server's state files, so they run as the user that owns the archive directory (the server's user), or as root.

What to do. Run the command with sudo, or the way your setup provides, with the server's -archive-dir (see Commands): sudo healthkit-relay pair -archive-dir /var/lib/healthkit-relay, docker compose exec relay healthkit-relay pair, or sudo healthkit-relay-ctl pair on NixOS.

Check. The command prints its result: a QR code for pair, a table for devices.

docs.title: The server stops at start with a -token-file error
docs.text:
What you see. The server exits right after it starts, and the last log line names -token-file: the file cannot be read, or its token is shorter than 16 characters.

Why. -token-file (HKR_TOKEN_FILE) is a setting from earlier versions, where you made the server token by hand. At start, the server imports that token as the admin token. A missing file is skipped; a file the server's user cannot read, or a token under 16 characters, stops it.

What to do.

  1. If the server has started with this version before, admin.json already holds the admin token: remove -token-file (or HKR_TOKEN_FILE) from the settings and delete the file.
  2. Otherwise, make the file readable by the server's user, or put the old token back in it, and start the server once so it imports it. Then remove the setting and delete the file.

Check. The server keeps running, and its log has no -token-file warning.

docs.title: Other computers cannot connect
docs.text:
What you see. The server answers on the server itself (curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz prints ok), but a browser or curl on another computer gets Failed to connect or waits until it gives up.

Why. The binary, the systemd unit and the NixOS module listen on 127.0.0.1:8080 by default: only the server itself reaches that address. The Docker image listens on every network interface.

What to do.

  1. Listen on every interface: HKR_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:8080 in /etc/healthkit-relay/env (Linux binary), or listen = "0.0.0.0:8080"; and openFirewall = true; on NixOS. Restart the server.
  2. Open port 8080 in the host's firewall: sudo ufw allow 8080/tcp, or sudo firewall-cmd --add-port=8080/tcp.

Check. From another computer, curl http://192.168.1.10:8080/healthz (with your server's address) prints ok.

docs.title: "permission denied" on the data directory (Docker)
docs.text:
What you see. The container stops, and docker compose logs relay shows permission denied on /data.

Why. ./data belongs to another user than the one the container runs as.

What to do. See Docker & Compose.

Check. docker compose ps shows relay as Up.

docs.title: Uploads fail with 413
docs.text:
What you see. The app's status names 413.

Why. A batch was larger than the server's -max-body-bytes (32 MB by default), or than your reverse proxy allows.

What to do. Allow 32 MB request bodies at the reverse proxy, e.g. client_max_body_size 32m; in nginx, and reload it.

Check. In the app, tap Sync Now: it ends with Up to date.

docs.title: The setup page shows "Set the server address"
docs.text:
What you see. The setup page shows Set the server address instead of a QR code.

Why. The page was opened at an address an iPhone cannot reach, such as 127.0.0.1 or localhost, and the server found no other address it answers on.

What to do. One of:

  • open the setup page with the address the iPhone uses, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup;
  • start the server with -public-url (HKR_PUBLIC_URL) set to the server address;
  • start the server with -listen 0.0.0.0:8080, so the page can offer the computer's network addresses.

Check. The page shows Pair your iPhone and a QR code.

docs.title: The setup page answers 403, or a message about private networks
docs.text:
What you see. Opening /setup gives a short page about private networks, with status 403.

Why. By default (-setup-from private), the setup page and pairing answer private networks only: your home network and Tailscale. Behind a reverse proxy on another host, the server sees the proxy's address, which may be public.

What to do.

  • From outside your home, pair over a VPN such as Tailscale, or at home.
  • Behind a reverse proxy, run the proxy on the same host as the server, or pair with healthkit-relay pair on the server.

Check. The setup page asks for the Admin token.

docs.title: The setup code expired or was already used
docs.text:
What you see. The app or the setup page says the setup code expired or was already used.

Why. A setup code pairs one iPhone, once, within 15 minutes.

What to do. Make a new one: reload the setup page, or run healthkit-relay pair again. To send the setup code's link to a phone that will open it later, make one that lasts longer: healthkit-relay pair -valid 2h.

Check. The app shows the server's address and asks you to Connect.

docs.title: The Camera shows no "Open in Health Relay"
docs.text:
What you see. The iPhone's Camera sees the QR code but offers no Open in Health Relay button.

Why. The setup code's QR code opens the Health Relay app, and the app is not installed on that iPhone.

What to do. Install the app, open it once, then scan the code again.

Check. The Camera shows Open in Health Relay.

docs.title: The first sync takes hours
docs.text:
What you see. The app shows Syncing for a long time after pairing.

Why. The first sync uploads your whole history, which can be hundreds of thousands of samples.

What to do. Keep the app open and the phone unlocked and charging. If the sync stops, it continues where it stopped. On iOS 26 and later, a first sync, or a Sync Now after hours without a sync, also goes on when you switch to another app: iOS shows its progress in a Live Activity, where you can stop it. Locking the iPhone pauses it, since Health data is locked then; it goes on after you unlock.

Check. The app shows Up to date.

docs.title: No syncs in the background
docs.text:
What you see. The app syncs when you open it, and at no other time.

Why. Health Relay syncs in the background several times a day; open the app to sync right away. iOS decides when to wake the app: after new Health data arrives, at its background app refresh, while the iPhone charges, and for about 30 seconds after you leave the app. Low Power Mode, closing the app from the app switcher, and Background App Refresh turned off all hold these wakes back. iPhone keeps Health data locked while the phone is locked, so a wake while it is locked sends nothing new: it notes a sync as owed, and the first wake after an unlock (or opening the app) sends everything since. With Tailscale, the iPhone reaches the server in the background only with VPN On Demand.

What to do.

  1. Turn on Background App Refresh: Settings › General › Background App Refresh, for Health Relay.
  2. Leave the app in the app switcher, and Low Power Mode off.
  3. With Tailscale, turn on VPN On Demand in the Tailscale app.

Check. The server's log says what started each batch, e.g. batch v2: … trigger observer, app background, and healthkit_relay_batches_total{trigger} counts them. Triggers other than foreground mean iOS woke the app.

From app 0.6.2 and server 0.6.2, the app also sends a heartbeat at the end of each background wake, even when it could read or send nothing. The server logs one line per heartbeat:

heartbeat: device eae02a2e, app 0.6.4 (11), trigger refresh, background, protected data unavailable, outcome locked, on battery, 0 uploaded in 0.2s, 28s background time left, owes a sync (locked), process 5h0m0s old; wakes: observer 3 (last 10-20 08:12:40), refresh 5 (last 10-20 13:05:11)
  • The trigger says what woke the app: observer (new Health data), refresh (background app refresh), processing (the processing task while charging), urlsession (an upload left under way finished, from app 0.7.0), unlock (the first unlock after a skipped sync), backgrounded (you left the app), continued (a sync you started that went on outside the app, iOS 26) and retry (after a failure). Server 0.7.0 counts each under its own name; older servers count the new ones as unknown.
  • protected data unavailable and outcome locked: the iPhone was locked; the sync waits for a wake after an unlock.
  • plugged in or on battery, then low power mode and background app refresh denied when they apply (app 0.6.4 and server 0.6.4): what iOS weighs before it wakes the app. Wakes that come only while plugged in mean iOS is holding the app's background work for the charger.
  • outcome upload failed or cancelled, or a last error: the app read Health but could not send everything in the time iOS gave it. The next wake sends the rest.
  • No heartbeat at all for hours: iOS did not wake the app. See the steps above.

healthkit_relay_last_heartbeat_timestamp_seconds{trigger} and healthkit_relay_last_batch_timestamp_seconds{trigger} give the time of the last of each, and refused tokens are logged with the client's address and user agent (refused: POST /v1/samples from …, 401, …).

docs.title: The app shows the server as not reachable on a home network
docs.text:
What you see. The app shows Not reachable right now while the iPhone is on the same Wi-Fi as the server.

Why. The app needs iOS's Local Network permission to reach addresses on your home network. Also, iOS allows plain http:// only to IP addresses (192.168.1.10) and .local names; other names need https://.

What to do.

  1. Allow it: Settings › Privacy & Security › Local Network › Health Relay.
  2. Check the server address in the app (the gear, Server address). With plain http://, use an IP address or a .local name, or set up HTTPS: see Networking & HTTPS.

Check. In the app, tap Sync Now: it ends with Up to date.

docs.title: The app shows "Disconnected"
docs.text:
What you see. The app shows Disconnected and asks you to scan a setup code from the setup page.

Why. The server no longer knows this iPhone's token: the paired device was revoked, or the server's archive directory was replaced (for example by an older backup or a new install).

What to do. Pair the iPhone again.

Check. The app shows Up to date, and the setup page lists the iPhone under Paired devices.

docs.title: A data type is missing
docs.text:
What you see. A type you have in Apple Health is not on the server.

Why. Health access is granted type by type. Some types are granted item by item (vision prescriptions, medications; in builds of your own, clinical documents and Health Records). Types your iOS version does not have are skipped.

What to do.

  1. In the app, tap the gear, then Data types read: it lists what the app reads.
  2. For the types granted item by item, tap each one under Shared item by item and pick the items to share.
  3. After an app update adds types, the app asks for Health access again on its own: allow them.

Check. After the next sync, GET /v1/types?present=true in the query API, or a DuckDB query, lists the type.

docs.title: Data is in the archive but not in Grafana
docs.text:
What you see. DuckDB or the query API shows the data; Grafana shows nothing, or only the last month.

Why. The server forwards numbers only, and only new ones: what it stores after -forward-url is set. A metrics database with a short retention drops older history (VictoriaMetrics keeps one month by default).

What to do.

  1. Check healthkit_relay_forward_errors_total on /metrics and the server's log for forwarding errors.
  2. Give the metrics database a long retention, e.g. -retentionPeriod=100y for VictoriaMetrics.
  3. To forward the history the server already holds, see Grafana.

Check. In Grafana, Explore shows healthkit_heart_rate back to your first data.

docs.title: /docs answers 404
docs.text:
What you see. http://192.168.1.10:8080/docs shows 404 page not found.

Why. The query API is off: the server starts it only with -query-duckdb.

What to do. Turn it on.

Check. /docs shows Health Relay query API, and the server's log has a line that starts with query API on:.

docs.title: A query answers 401 or 403
docs.text:
What you see. {"error":"unauthorized"} (status 401), or an error about the kind of token (status 403).

Why. 401: the server does not know the token. It was mistyped, cut short, or revoked. 403: the token is a paired device's token, which uploads and does not query.

What to do. Create a read token and paste the whole of it, after Authorization: Bearer.

Check. curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://192.168.1.10:8080/v1/types answers {"types":[....

docs.title: A query answers 400 "unknown type"
docs.text:
What you see. e.g. {"error":"unknown type HKQuantityTypeIdentifierSteps; did you mean HKQuantityTypeIdentifierStepCount?"}.

Why. The type in the address is not one of HealthKit's identifiers.

What to do. Use the name the message suggests, or pick one from GET /v1/types.

Check. The same request answers with data.

docs.title: Today's data is missing from queries
docs.text:
What you see. The app is Up to date, but the query API or DuckDB lacks the last hour.

Why. The server writes new samples to Parquet at the hourly flush; the query API and DuckDB read Parquet.

What to do. Wait for the next flush (at most an hour, -flush-interval).

Check. The same query, an hour later, includes the samples.

docs.title: A query answers 422, 503 or 504
docs.text:
What you see. An error with status 422 (the answer is too large), 503 (too many queries at once) or 504 (the query took too long).

Why. The server bounds each query: -query-max-rows, -query-concurrency and -query-timeout (see Settings).

What to do. 422 and 504: ask for a shorter range, a smaller limit, or leave out raw. 503: try again after a few seconds.

Check. The query answers 200 with data.

docs.title: The log says the test query failed
docs.text:
What you see. At start, the server's log has a line with the test query failed, and every query answers 500. Or the server stops at start with an error that names -query-duckdb.

Why. duckdb could not run or could not read the archive. The end of the log line gives the reason, e.g. a DuckDB version before 1.2, or a folder the server's user cannot read. When the server stops at start, -query-duckdb names a file that is not there.

What to do. Install duckdb 1.2 or newer, check that the path in -query-duckdb is right, and that -query-archive-dir, if set, is readable by the server's user. Restart the server.

Check. The log shows query API on: with no failed test query after it.

docs.title: Still stuck?
docs.text: Open an issue with the versions, how the server runs and the relevant log lines. Leave out health data and tokens.

docs.title: Setup guides
docs.text:
The server is the healthkit-relay program. It runs on a computer you keep on and receives your iPhone's Health data. Pick the guide for that computer and follow it from top to bottom. New to these words? The glossary explains server address, setup page, admin token and the rest, each with an example.

Your computer Guide Any Linux or macOS machine with Docker (the easiest start) Docker & Compose A Linux server or a VPS (virtual private server) Linux binary + systemd A NixOS machine NixOS A Mac that stays on macOS (launchd) A NAS: Synology, Unraid or TrueNAS Synology, Unraid, TrueNAS A Raspberry Pi or another 64-bit ARM board Raspberry Pi & ARM

The server is one self-contained program, published as:

  • a Docker image, ghcr.io/leblancfg/healthkit-relay, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64, with a Compose file;
  • release archives for Linux, macOS and FreeBSD on amd64 and arm64, with a systemd unit, on the releases page;
  • a Nix flake, github:leblancfg/healthkit-relay, with a package and a NixOS module.

The Docker Compose, binary + systemd and NixOS setups are tested end to end in CI (continuous integration, the tests that run on every change): the server is installed as these guides say, then a test pairs like the app, uploads a batch, checks that it is stored, restarts the server and checks that the batch is still there.

docs.title: What every setup needs
docs.text:
• An archive: the folder where the server keeps your data. Put it on a disk with room to grow, and include it in your backups. Each guide names it, e.g. ./data with Docker Compose.
  • The admin token: the password of your server. The server makes it on its first start and prints it once, in its log. Save it in a password manager: it signs in to the setup page. The archive keeps only its SHA-256 hash, in admin.json, and healthkit-relay admin reset makes a new one.
  • A server address: the address your iPhone uses to reach the server, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080 on your home Wi-Fi. Networking & HTTPS shows how to reach it from anywhere.

docs.title: Check your setup
docs.text:
Each guide ends with the server running. These steps check it, whichever guide you followed.

  1. On the computer running the server, ask it whether it answers:

    curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz

    It prints ok.

  2. Read the admin token in the server's log:

    Setup Command Docker Compose docker compose logs relay Docker without Compose docker logs healthkit-relay systemd, NixOS sudo journalctl -u healthkit-relay macOS cat ~/Library/Logs/healthkit-relay.log NAS the container's log in the NAS's web interface

    The log shows the admin token and the setup page's address:

        Admin token: BBvGW16otZlTAfIc7RbrNmMVd7PXBVU8skBFvHZhO_4
    Setup page:  http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup

  3. Open the setup page in a browser on a computer on the same network, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup. The page shows Sign in and an Admin token field.

  4. Pair your iPhone: follow Pairing an iPhone.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Every flag has an environment variable: HKR_ plus the flag name in upper case, with dashes as underscores. For example, -archive-dir /data and HKR_ARCHIVE_DIR=/data do the same. When both are set, the flag wins.

Flag Default -listen 127.0.0.1:8080 address and port to listen on. 127.0.0.1:8080 answers this computer only (for a reverse proxy or Tailscale); 0.0.0.0:8080 also answers other machines on your network. The Docker image sets :8080 -archive-dir required the archive: staging.db, parquet/, admin.json, devices.json, codes.json -public-url the server address, put in setup codes, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080 or https://health.example.com. Unset, the setup page offers the addresses it finds -setup-from private who may open the setup page and pair: private (this computer, your home network, Tailscale), any or off -forward-url line-protocol write URL to forward numeric samples to a metrics database (see Grafana) -forward-token-file file holding a bearer token for -forward-url -measurement healthkit line-protocol measurement name -query-duckdb (off) the duckdb program, which turns on the query API; the -query-... flags are listed there -max-body-bytes 33554432 largest request the server accepts, in bytes (32 MiB) -flush-interval 1h how often staged records are written to Parquet -compact-at 03:30 local time of the nightly compaction, HH:MM -group-read off make the archive readable by the service's group (0750/0640), for backups or queries -token-file deprecated: the server token file of earlier versions, imported into admin.json at start; delete the file once imported -version print the version and exit

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
The same program has commands for pairing and tokens. They take the same flags and HKR_ variables as the server.

These change the files in the archive (admin.json, devices.json, codes.json), with the server running or stopped. The server rereads the files when they change, so a command takes effect at once.

Command What it does pair prints a setup code as a QR code in the terminal, valid 15 minutes; -valid 2h makes it last longer, up to 24h devices lists paired devices and read tokens, with their IDs revoke <id> revokes a paired device or a read token, e.g. revoke 3f9a1c2e token create -name <name> prints a new read token for the query API, e.g. -name grafana admin reset prints a new admin token; the old one stops working at once

Run them as the server's user or as root, for example:

docker compose exec relay healthkit-relay pair                  # Docker Compose
sudo healthkit-relay-ctl pair                                   # NixOS
sudo healthkit-relay pair -archive-dir /var/lib/healthkit-relay \
  -public-url http://192.168.1.10:8080                          # systemd

These work on the archive with the server stopped:

Command What it does migrate converts the JSON Lines archive of versions before 0.5 flush writes staged records to Parquet now (the hourly job) compact merges each partition's Parquet files now (the nightly job)

healthkit-relay -help lists every flag, and the server README describes each command.

docs.title: Docker & Compose
docs.text:
Docker runs the server in a container: a packaged program with everything it needs. Docker Compose starts it from a docker-compose.yml file that holds its settings. This guide works on any Linux or macOS machine with Docker; the Quick start follows the same steps with more detail on each.

The image ghcr.io/leblancfg/healthkit-relay runs on linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. It holds the server and a health check, on a distroless base (a minimal image with only what the program needs). It runs as a non-root user, 65532 unless you choose another, and keeps its archive in /data.

Tag What latest the latest release X.Y.Z, e.g. 0.7.0 one release X.Y, e.g. 0.7 the latest patch release of that minor line X the latest release of that major line (from 1.0 on) edge, sha-<commit> the main branch, between releases

To choose when you update, pin a version: HKR_VERSION=0.7.0 in .env (see below).

The image sets HKR_LISTEN=:8080 and HKR_ARCHIVE_DIR=/data, so you mount the archive at /data and set the server address. Every other flag can be set as an HKR_ variable.

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
The repository's docker-compose.yml is the supported setup, and the one CI tests end to end. Replace 192.168.1.10 with the IP address of the computer running Docker (hostname -I on Linux, ipconfig getifaddr en0 on macOS).

  1. Make a folder for the server and go into it:

    mkdir -p ~/healthkit-relay && cd ~/healthkit-relay

  2. Download the Compose file, make the archive folder data and write your settings to .env:

    curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leblancfg/healthkit-relay/main/docker-compose.yml
mkdir -p data
printf 'HKR_USER=%s\nHKR_PUBLIC_URL=%s\n' "$(id -u):$(id -g)" http://192.168.1.10:8080 > .env

    cat .env shows two lines, e.g. HKR_USER=1000:1000 and HKR_PUBLIC_URL=http://192.168.1.10:8080.

  3. Start the server:

    docker compose up -d

    The last line ends with Started. After a few seconds, docker compose ps shows the container as healthy: it answers http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz.

  4. Read the admin token, which the server prints once, on its first start:

    docker compose logs relay

    The log shows it, with the setup page's address:

    relay-1  |     Admin token: BBvGW16otZlTAfIc7RbrNmMVd7PXBVU8skBFvHZhO_4
relay-1  |     Setup page:  http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup

    Save the admin token in a password manager: it signs in to the setup page.

  5. Pair your iPhone. Open http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup and sign in with the admin token, or print the QR code in the terminal:

    docker compose exec relay healthkit-relay pair

    Then follow Pairing an iPhone.

The other commands run the same way, in the server's folder:

docker compose exec relay healthkit-relay devices                  # paired devices and read tokens
docker compose exec relay healthkit-relay revoke 3f9a1c2e
docker compose exec relay healthkit-relay token create -name grafana
docker compose exec relay healthkit-relay admin reset              # a new admin token

admin reset prints a new admin token, and the old one stops working at once.

The service is called relay. It reads these settings from .env:

Variable HKR_USER required: the uid:gid (user and group IDs) the server runs as. Use your own, so that ./data stays yours and is backed up with the folder HKR_PUBLIC_URL required: the server address, put in setup codes, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080 or https://health.example.com HKR_VERSION image tag, default latest; e.g. HKR_VERSION=0.7.0 to pin HKR_PORT port on the host, default 8080 HKR_FORWARD_URL optional: forward numeric samples to a metrics database (below)

./data is the archive. It holds your data and the server's state: staging.db, parquet/, admin.json, devices.json and codes.json.

The server address in a container

Inside a container, the server sees the container's own network, so it learns the server address from HKR_PUBLIC_URL. The Compose file requires it. Open the setup page at that same address, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup.

docs.title: With VictoriaMetrics and Grafana
docs.text:
The same Compose file has a metrics profile. It adds VictoriaMetrics, a time-series database, with a retention of 100 years, and Grafana, with VictoriaMetrics already set up as its data source. Add the forward URL to .env and start with the profile:

echo HKR_FORWARD_URL=http://victoriametrics:8428/influx/write >> .env
docker compose --profile metrics up -d

Grafana is on http://localhost:3000, on this computer only. GRAFANA_PORT in .env changes the port. The first login is admin, password admin: Grafana then asks for a new password. To open Grafana from other computers, set that password first, then add GRAFANA_BIND=0.0.0.0 to .env and run docker compose --profile metrics up -d again. See Grafana for queries. The long retention matters: the first sync sends years of history, and a database with a short retention drops most of it. VictoriaMetrics and Grafana keep their data in the Docker volumes victoriametrics and grafana.

docs.title: Without Compose
docs.text:
mkdir -p data
docker run -d --name healthkit-relay --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 8080:8080 --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -e HKR_PUBLIC_URL=http://192.168.1.10:8080 \
  -v "$PWD/data:/data" \
  ghcr.io/leblancfg/healthkit-relay:latest
docker logs healthkit-relay                         # the admin token
docker exec healthkit-relay healthkit-relay pair    # the QR code for the iPhone

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
In the server's folder:

docker compose pull && docker compose up -d

With HKR_VERSION pinned, change it in .env first. The server upgrades the archive in place when it starts; back it up before you update across minor versions, e.g. from 0.6 to 0.7.

From 0.6 and earlier, where you made a ./token file by hand and mounted it at /run/secrets/hkr_token: on the first start of this version, the server imports the token's hash into data/admin.json and logs a deprecation warning. The same token is now your admin token and signs in to the setup page. Save it in a password manager, then delete ./token and remove its mount from your docker-compose.yml. Paired devices keep their tokens. An app you set up by hand with the old token: pair it again from the setup page.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
If the server cannot write /data, the folder ./data belongs to another user than the one the container runs as.

  • With Compose, that user is HKR_USER: set it to the owner of ./data, which stat -c %u:%g data prints on Linux (stat -f %u:%g data on macOS), e.g. 1000:1000.
  • With docker run, pass the same with --user. Without --user the image runs as 65532:65532, which can write a Docker volume but not a folder you own.

docs.title: Linux binary + systemd
docs.text: This guide runs the server directly on a Linux server or VPS (virtual private server), amd64 or arm64, as a systemd service. systemd is the program that starts and watches services on most Linux distributions: Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, Arch and others.

docs.title: Install the binary
docs.text:
Each release has an archive per platform, healthkit-relay_X.Y.Z_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz, and a checksums.txt with their SHA-256 checksums. The Linux archive holds the server, the systemd unit packaging/healthkit-relay.service, the READMEs and the license.

  1. Open a root shell:

    sudo -i

  2. Download the archive for your machine, check it and install the server. Set VERSION to the newest version on the releases page:

    VERSION=0.7.0
ARCH=$(uname -m | sed 's/x86_64/amd64/;s/aarch64/arm64/')
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
curl -fLO "https://github.com/leblancfg/healthkit-relay/releases/download/v${VERSION}/healthkit-relay_${VERSION}_linux_${ARCH}.tar.gz"
curl -fLO "https://github.com/leblancfg/healthkit-relay/releases/download/v${VERSION}/checksums.txt"
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt
tar -xzf "healthkit-relay_${VERSION}_linux_${ARCH}.tar.gz"
install -m 755 healthkit-relay /usr/local/bin/
healthkit-relay -version

    sha256sum prints OK after the archive's name, and the last command prints the version, e.g. 0.7.0.

To build from source instead, with Go: make server-build writes bin/healthkit-relay, and the unit is in the repository's packaging/ folder.

docs.title: Run it as a service
docs.text:
Still as root, in the folder where you unpacked the archive:

  1. Install the unit and make the settings folder:

    install -m 644 packaging/healthkit-relay.service /etc/systemd/system/
install -d -m 700 /etc/healthkit-relay

  2. Write the settings file, /etc/healthkit-relay/env. Pick the case that fits:

    Home networkTailscale or reverse proxy (HTTPS)

    The iPhone syncs when it is on your home Wi-Fi. Replace 192.168.1.10 with the machine's IP address (hostname -I prints it):

    cat > /etc/healthkit-relay/env <<'EOF'
HKR_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:8080
HKR_PUBLIC_URL=http://192.168.1.10:8080
EOF

    If the machine has a firewall, open port 8080 to your network, e.g. with ufw: ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 8080 proto tcp.

    The iPhone syncs from anywhere, over HTTPS. The server listens on 127.0.0.1:8080, and Tailscale or a reverse proxy publishes it: see Networking & HTTPS. Use your HTTPS address:

    echo HKR_PUBLIC_URL=https://health.example.com > /etc/healthkit-relay/env

  3. Start the service, now and at every boot:

    systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl enable --now healthkit-relay
systemctl status healthkit-relay

    systemctl status shows active (running).

  4. Read the admin token, which the server prints once, on its first start:

    journalctl -u healthkit-relay

    The journal shows it, with the setup page's address:

        Admin token: BBvGW16otZlTAfIc7RbrNmMVd7PXBVU8skBFvHZhO_4
    Setup page:  http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup

    Save the admin token in a password manager: it signs in to the setup page.

  5. Pair your iPhone: open the setup page and sign in with the admin token, or run pair (see Commands). Then follow Pairing an iPhone.

docs.title: What the unit sets up
docs.text:
The unit (packaging/healthkit-relay.service) runs the server as a dynamic user (a user systemd makes for the service), in a sandbox, with:

  • the archive in /var/lib/healthkit-relay, mode 0700: staging.db, parquet/, admin.json, devices.json and codes.json. systemd keeps it in /var/lib/private/healthkit-relay, and /var/lib/healthkit-relay is a link to it;

  • its settings read from /etc/healthkit-relay/env, one HKR_<FLAG>=value per line (see Configuration), e.g.:

    /etc/healthkit-relay/env
    HKR_PUBLIC_URL=https://health.example.com
# HKR_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:8080                             # iPhones on the home network
# HKR_FORWARD_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8428/influx/write  # metrics, see Grafana

  • HKR_LISTEN=127.0.0.1:8080 unless the env file sets another address: the server then answers only this machine, for a reverse proxy or tailscale serve.

After you edit the env file, run systemctl restart healthkit-relay. To change what the env file cannot, such as the paths, run systemctl edit healthkit-relay: it keeps your changes in a separate file, so an update can replace the unit.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
pair prints a setup code as a QR code in the terminal. Run it as root, with the archive:

sudo healthkit-relay pair -archive-dir /var/lib/healthkit-relay -public-url http://192.168.1.10:8080

The commands read their settings from flags and the environment of your shell, and /etc/healthkit-relay/env belongs to the service. So give pair the server address with -public-url, the same as HKR_PUBLIC_URL in the env file.

devices, revoke <id>, token create -name grafana and admin reset take the same -archive-dir. admin reset prints a new admin token, and the old one stops working at once. Files the commands write keep the owner of the archive, so the service can still read them.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
1. Download the new archive and check it as in Install the binary.

  2. Install the server and the unit again, then restart:

    install -m 755 healthkit-relay /usr/local/bin/
install -m 644 packaging/healthkit-relay.service /etc/systemd/system/
systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart healthkit-relay

From 0.6 and earlier, with an /etc/healthkit-relay/token: before the restart, uncomment the two lines LoadCredential= and Environment=HKR_TOKEN_FILE= in the new unit. On its next start, the server imports the token's hash into admin.json, and the token keeps working as the admin token. Once it has started, delete the token file, comment those two lines again, and restart. If you skip this, the server makes a new admin token and prints it to the journal.

docs.title: macOS (launchd)
docs.text:
A Mac mini, or any Mac that stays on, can run the server, on Apple silicon or Intel. launchd, the macOS service manager, starts it when you log in and restarts it if it stops.

Replace 192.168.1.10 below with your Mac's IP address. To find it:

ipconfig getifaddr en0    # e.g. 192.168.1.10

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
1. Download healthkit-relay_<version>_darwin_arm64.tar.gz from the releases page, or _amd64 on an Intel Mac. About This Mac tells you which one you have: an Apple M chip is Apple silicon (arm64).

  2. In Terminal, in the folder you downloaded it to, unpack and install the server:

    tar xzf healthkit-relay_*_darwin_*.tar.gz healthkit-relay
xattr -d com.apple.quarantine healthkit-relay 2>/dev/null   # lets macOS run a downloaded program
sudo mkdir -p /usr/local/bin
sudo install -m 755 healthkit-relay /usr/local/bin/
healthkit-relay -version

    The last command prints the version, e.g. 0.7.0.

With Nix, nix profile install github:leblancfg/healthkit-relay installs it instead.

docs.title: Run it at login
docs.text:
1. Make the archive, the folder where the server keeps your data:

    mkdir -p ~/Library/Application\ Support/healthkit-relay/data

  2. Write the launchd agent, a file that tells launchd how to run the server. This command writes it with your home folder and server address filled in:

    mkdir -p ~/Library/LaunchAgents
cat > ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.github.healthkit-relay.plist <<EOF
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>Label</key><string>io.github.healthkit-relay</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
  <array>
    <string>/usr/local/bin/healthkit-relay</string>
    <string>-listen</string><string>0.0.0.0:8080</string>
    <string>-public-url</string><string>http://192.168.1.10:8080</string>
    <string>-archive-dir</string><string>$HOME/Library/Application Support/healthkit-relay/data</string>
  </array>
  <key>RunAtLoad</key><true/>
  <key>KeepAlive</key><true/>
  <key>StandardOutPath</key><string>$HOME/Library/Logs/healthkit-relay.log</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key><string>$HOME/Library/Logs/healthkit-relay.log</string>
</dict>
</plist>
EOF

  3. Start it:

    launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.github.healthkit-relay.plist
launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/io.github.healthkit-relay | grep state

    The second command prints state = running. If the macOS firewall is on, macOS asks whether healthkit-relay may accept incoming connections: click Allow.

  4. Read the admin token, which the server prints once, on its first start:

    cat ~/Library/Logs/healthkit-relay.log

    The log shows it, with the setup page's address:

        Admin token: BBvGW16otZlTAfIc7RbrNmMVd7PXBVU8skBFvHZhO_4
    Setup page:  http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup

    Save the admin token in a password manager: it signs in to the setup page.

  5. Pair your iPhone: open http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup and sign in with the admin token, or print the QR code (see below). Then follow Pairing an iPhone.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
The commands run as you, on the same archive. Give them the server address with -public-url:

healthkit-relay pair -archive-dir ~/Library/Application\ Support/healthkit-relay/data \
  -public-url http://192.168.1.10:8080
healthkit-relay admin reset -archive-dir ~/Library/Application\ Support/healthkit-relay/data   # a new admin token

To restart the server after an update: launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/io.github.healthkit-relay.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Keep the Mac awake: in System Settings › Energy, turn on Prevent automatic sleeping when the display is off. While the Mac sleeps, syncs wait until it wakes.
  • Give the Mac a fixed address with a DHCP reservation in your router, so the server address stays the same.
  • A user agent runs while you are logged in. To run the server with nobody logged in, put the plist in /Library/LaunchDaemons/ with a UserName key, owned by root, and load it with sudo launchctl bootstrap system ....
  • Time Machine backs up the archive with the rest of your home folder.

docs.title: Synology, Unraid, TrueNAS
docs.text: On a NAS (network-attached storage), run the server's Docker image from the NAS's container app. A NAS makes a good home for the archive: it is on all the time, has redundant disks and often has backups already.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The settings are the same on every NAS. Replace 192.168.1.10 with the NAS's IP address.

Setting Value Image ghcr.io/leblancfg/healthkit-relay:latest, or a version tag, e.g. 0.7.0 Port container 8080 → host 8080 (or another free port) Folder a shared folder for the archive, e.g. /volume1/docker/healthkit-relay/data → /data HKR_PUBLIC_URL the server address, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080, or your HTTPS address User the owner of the archive folder, as uid:gid (see below) Restart policy unless stopped

The image already sets HKR_LISTEN=:8080 and HKR_ARCHIVE_DIR=/data.

The user. The container runs as user 65532 unless you set another, and that user cannot write a folder you own. Run it as the folder's owner: over SSH, id prints your IDs, e.g. uid=1026(you) gid=100(users) gives 1026:100. Or give the folder to 65532: chown -R 65532:65532 /volume1/docker/healthkit-relay/data.

The admin token. On its first start the server makes the admin token and prints it once, in the container's log (the log view of the NAS's container app, or docker logs over SSH):

    Admin token: BBvGW16otZlTAfIc7RbrNmMVd7PXBVU8skBFvHZhO_4
    Setup page:  http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup

Save it in a password manager: it signs in to the setup page. The archive holds its hash (admin.json) and the hashes of the paired devices' tokens (devices.json): share the archive folder with nobody else over SMB or NFS.

The NAS guides below use this Compose file. Write your user and server address in it:

docker-compose.yml
services:
  relay:
    image: ghcr.io/leblancfg/healthkit-relay:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    user: "1026:100"
    ports:
      - 8080:8080
    environment:
      HKR_PUBLIC_URL: http://192.168.1.10:8080
    volumes:
      - ./data:/data

docs.title: Synology DSM 7 (Container Manager)
docs.text:
1. In Package Center, install Container Manager.
  2. In File Station, create the folder docker/healthkit-relay/data.
  3. In Container Manager, open Project › Create. Set the path to docker/healthkit-relay, and create or upload the docker-compose.yml above. Finish the wizard. The project starts.
  4. Open the project's log and find the admin token.
  5. Open http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup and sign in with the admin token. Then follow Pairing an iPhone.

For HTTPS on a Synology, the built-in reverse proxy (Control Panel › Login Portal › Advanced › Reverse Proxy) can forward https://health.example.com to localhost:8080. Or install the Tailscale package (see Networking & HTTPS).

docs.title: Unraid
docs.text:
1. In the Docker tab, click Add Container. Set Repository to ghcr.io/leblancfg/healthkit-relay:latest and Network Type to bridge.
  2. Add a Port 8080 → 8080, a Path /mnt/user/appdata/healthkit-relay/data → /data, and a Variable HKR_PUBLIC_URL with the server address. Unraid's appdata share belongs to 99:100 (nobody:users): switch to the advanced view and add --user 99:100 under Extra Parameters.
  3. Click Apply. The container starts.
  4. Open the container's log and find the admin token.
  5. Open http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup and sign in with the admin token. Then follow Pairing an iPhone.

The Appdata Backup plugin backs up the appdata share, archive included.

docs.title: TrueNAS SCALE
docs.text:
1. Create a dataset for the archive, e.g. tank/apps/healthkit-relay.
  2. Open Apps › Discover Apps › Custom App. On recent versions you can use Install via YAML instead, with the Compose file above and the full path of the dataset in place of ./data.
  3. Set the image ghcr.io/leblancfg/healthkit-relay with the tag latest or a version, the variable HKR_PUBLIC_URL, the port 8080, the host path /mnt/tank/apps/healthkit-relay → /data, and the user and group IDs that own the dataset.
  4. Open the app's logs and find the admin token.
  5. Open http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup and sign in with the admin token. Then follow Pairing an iPhone.
  6. Snapshot the dataset on a schedule: that is your backup on the NAS.

If the container cannot write the archive folder, give the folder to the user the container runs as (see Docker & Compose).

docs.title: NixOS
docs.text: The repository is a flake with the server package and a NixOS module, nixosModules.default. The module runs the server as a hardened systemd service.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
1. Add the flake as an input of your system's flake.nix, import the module and turn on the service. This example is for a server on your home network, at 192.168.1.10:

    flake.nix
    {
  inputs.nixpkgs.url = "github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable";
  inputs.healthkit-relay.url = "github:leblancfg/healthkit-relay";
  inputs.healthkit-relay.inputs.nixpkgs.follows = "nixpkgs";

  outputs = { nixpkgs, healthkit-relay, ... }: {
    nixosConfigurations.myhost = nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem {
      system = "x86_64-linux";
      modules = [
        ./configuration.nix
        healthkit-relay.nixosModules.default
        {
          services.healthkit-relay = {
            enable = true;
            publicUrl = "http://192.168.1.10:8080";
            listen = "0.0.0.0:8080";
            openFirewall = true;
            # forwardUrl = "http://127.0.0.1:8428/influx/write";
          };
        }
      ];
    };
  };
}

    With Tailscale or a reverse proxy instead (see Networking & HTTPS), set publicUrl to your HTTPS address, e.g. "https://health.example.com", and leave listen and openFirewall at their defaults.

  2. Build and switch to the new configuration:

    sudo nixos-rebuild switch --flake .#myhost
systemctl status healthkit-relay

    systemctl status shows active (running).

  3. Read the admin token, which the service prints once, on its first start:

    sudo journalctl -u healthkit-relay

    The journal shows it, with the setup page's address:

        Admin token: BBvGW16otZlTAfIc7RbrNmMVd7PXBVU8skBFvHZhO_4
    Setup page:  http://192.168.1.10:8080/setup

    Save the admin token in a password manager: it signs in to the setup page.

  4. Pair your iPhone: open the setup page and sign in with the admin token, or print the QR code with sudo healthkit-relay-ctl pair. Then follow Pairing an iPhone.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
All under services.healthkit-relay:

Option Default enable false run the server package the flake's package the healthkit-relay package to run listen "127.0.0.1:8080" address and port to listen on; "0.0.0.0:8080" also answers iPhones on your home network publicUrl null the server address, put in setup codes. With null, the setup page offers the addresses it finds tokenFile null deprecated: the server token file of earlier versions, imported into admin.json at start (see below) setupFrom "private" who may open the setup page and pair: "private", "any" or "off" forwardUrl null line-protocol write URL to forward numeric samples to forwardTokenFile null file holding a bearer token for forwardUrl extraFlags [ ] extra server flags, e.g. [ "-measurement" "health" ] openFirewall false open the listen port in the firewall

The service runs as the system user healthkit-relay. Its archive is /var/lib/healthkit-relay, mode 0700: staging.db, parquet/, admin.json, devices.json and codes.json. systemd reads forwardTokenFile as a credential, so the file can stay owned by root with mode 600.

docs.title: The admin token
docs.text:
The service makes the admin token on its first start and prints it once, in the journal (sudo journalctl -u healthkit-relay). /var/lib/healthkit-relay/admin.json keeps its SHA-256 hash. sudo healthkit-relay-ctl admin reset prints a new one, and the old one stops working at once.

From earlier versions: the service imports a tokenFile, or the /var/lib/healthkit-relay/token the module made, into admin.json at start, and logs a warning. The token keeps working as the admin token. Once the service has started with this version, set tokenFile to null (or remove it) and delete the file.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
The module installs healthkit-relay-ctl, which runs healthkit-relay with the service's settings and archive. Run it as root:

sudo healthkit-relay-ctl pair                       # a setup code, as a QR code
sudo healthkit-relay-ctl devices                    # paired devices and read tokens
sudo healthkit-relay-ctl revoke 3f9a1c2e
sudo healthkit-relay-ctl token create -name grafana # a read token for the query API
sudo healthkit-relay-ctl admin reset                # a new admin token

healthkit-relay-pair is short for healthkit-relay-ctl pair.

docs.title: VictoriaMetrics
docs.text:
To forward numeric samples to VictoriaMetrics on the same machine, turn on its NixOS module and point the server at it:

services.victoriametrics = {
  enable = true;
  listenAddress = "127.0.0.1:8428";
  retentionPeriod = "100y";
};
services.healthkit-relay.forwardUrl = "http://127.0.0.1:8428/influx/write";

docs.title: Trying it
docs.text: To run the server without installing it: nix run github:leblancfg/healthkit-relay -- -help. nix flake check runs the module in a NixOS virtual machine with the end-to-end test.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi & ARM
docs.text:
The server runs well on a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5, or any board with a 64-bit ARM processor. It is a linux/arm64 program that uses little processor time and memory between syncs.

You need:

  • A 64-bit operating system: Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit), Ubuntu, DietPi... To check, run uname -m: it prints aarch64. The server runs on 64-bit ARM (arm64) only.
  • An SSD over USB for the archive, the folder where the server keeps your data. The first sync writes years of history, and an SD card wears out and corrupts under that many writes.

Then follow one of these guides:

  • Docker: install Docker with curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh, then follow Docker & Compose. The image runs on arm64, so the same Compose file works. Make the server's folder on the SSD, so that its data folder is on the SSD too.
  • Binary + systemd: follow Linux binary + systemd. Its script picks the arm64 archive by itself. The unit's archive is /var/lib/healthkit-relay, a link to /var/lib/private/healthkit-relay: mount the SSD, or a folder on it, at /var/lib/private/healthkit-relay before the first start.

To check the result, see Check your setup.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• The first sync is the heavy part: batches of up to 5,000 records, written to the archive and compressed into Parquet every hour. It takes longer than on a desktop computer. After that, syncs are small.
  • Give the Pi a fixed address with a DHCP reservation in your router, or use Tailscale, so the iPhone always finds it.
  • Watch the SSD's free space with df -h, or in Grafana.
